title: Composable design
description: How to extract stateful logic so it stays tied to the component that called it.

blocks.title: A composable is a function that owns reactive setup
blocks.content:
A composable is a function, usually named `useX`, that uses Vue APIs to create state and effects. It is not a component and it has no template. Call it synchronously during `setup` so `watch`, `computed`, and lifecycle hooks attach to the current instance and stop when that instance unmounts.

The function should accept reactive inputs as refs, getters, or `MaybeRefOrGetter` values and read them with `toValue()`. Accepting a raw boolean "freezes" the option at call time. Returning refs keeps the caller in control of `.value` in script and auto-unwrap in the template.
keyPoints: Call composables at the top level of setup, not after a later `await` and not inside an event handler, unless you manage an `effectScope` yourself.
Return refs and plain functions. Do not return a reactive object and also a pile of unrelated globals.
Accept getters when the input must stay live (`() => props.id`).
Side effects that touch the DOM belong in `onMounted` inside the composable, with cleanup in `onUnmounted`.

blocks.title: State inside the function is per caller
blocks.content:
Each call to `useCounter()` creates a new ref. That is what you want for a component instance. If two components must share the counter, the ref has to live outside the function, in a module singleton or a store. Hiding a singleton inside a composable that looks per-instance is a support incident: tests leak state, and two widgets move together.

Name the choice. `useLocalDraft()` creates state. `useSessionStore()` reads shared state. Do not do both in one function without saying so in the return value.
keyPoints: Per-call state is the default and the safe one.
Module-level refs are singletons shared by every caller in that JS realm.
SSR makes singletons especially dangerous: one server process can leak data between requests if the singleton holds user data.
Pass dependencies in. Importing the router or a store from inside a composable is fine when that really is the source, and it should be obvious.

blocks.title: A per-component interval with cleanup
blocks.explanation: Every caller gets its own `now` ref and its own timer. The watch reads the live `enabled` value through `toValue`. Unmount and a false flag both stop the interval.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: What makes a composable hard to maintain?
blocks.answer:
Hidden singletons, DOM queries for nodes the caller should have passed in, and effects registered after an await so they never stop. A composable that silently imports five stores is also hard to test. I want inputs as arguments, outputs as refs, and cleanup next to the subscription.

I also look for composables that return 20 fields. That is usually a component that never got a template. Split it, or make it a real component if the reuse is visual.
blocks.explanation: Reusability comes from an explicit input and output, not from moving code into a `use` function.

blocks.title: The shared ref in the module
blocks.question: Two `Player.vue` instances both call `useVolume()`. The implementation is `const volume = ref(1)` at module scope, and the function returns that same ref. A user drags the slider on one player. What happens to the other?
blocks.answer: Both players change. The ref was created once when the module evaluated, and every call returns it. Move `const volume = ref(1)` inside `useVolume()` for per-player state, or rename the function and document a shared session volume if sharing is intentional.
blocks.explanation:
Module scope is a singleton. Function scope runs per caller.

[Further reading](https://vuejs.org/guide/reusability/composables.html)
hints: How many times does the module-level `ref()` call run?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: You want one `useDocumentTitle(title)` used by every page. Titles from two mounted pages could fight during a transition, and SSR must not leak one user's title into another request. How do you write it?
blocks.answer:
Take the title as a getter. In the browser, write `document.title` from a watcher and reset it on unmount if this caller still owns the current title. Guard `document` so the server does not touch it. Do not store the title in a module singleton that survives requests. On the server, set the title through the SSR context or the meta framework's head API for this request only.

If two callers can be mounted during a transition, the composable needs an owner stack, not a single global string that the first unmount clears.
blocks.explanation: Browser singletons and server singletons fail differently. The API should make ownership explicit.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Starting a `watch` inside `onMounted` that closes over a prop value copied at click time.
blocks.whyItHappens: The effect lives, but it tracks the wrong data, or it is registered so late that tests never see it.
blocks.correctApproach: Create the watch during the composable call. Use `toValue` or a getter so each run reads the current prop.

blocks.title: Production guidance
blocks.content: A composable is a small stateful module with a start and a stop.
keyPoints: Call it synchronously in setup.
Create per-instance state inside the function.
Accept `MaybeRefOrGetter` inputs that must stay live.
Avoid request-scoped data in module singletons on the server.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- Composables set up state when called. They are not components.
- Synchronous setup calls attach effects to the instance.
- Module-level refs are shared by every caller.
- Return refs. Accept getters for live inputs.

Official references

- https://vuejs.org/guide/reusability/composables.html

title: Pinia stores
description: Setup stores, storeToRefs, and when a store outlives a component.

blocks.title: A store is shared state with a defined lifetime
blocks.content:
Pinia is the standard state library for Vue 3. `defineStore` returns a composable. The first call in an app creates the store; later calls return the same instance for that Pinia root. A setup store (a function that returns refs and functions) looks like any other composable, with the difference that the state is shared and shows up in Vue devtools.

Use a store for session data, cached server data, and UI state that several routes must see. Do not put a single input's draft in a store if only one component reads it. That draft can live in the component and disappear with it.
keyPoints: Setup stores and options stores both work. Setup stores compose naturally with other composables.
The store is created per Pinia instance, which matters in SSR and in tests.
Actions can be async. The store does not cancel them for you when the user navigates away.
Getters are cached like computed properties.

blocks.title: Destructuring a store drops reactivity unless you use storeToRefs
blocks.content:
A Pinia store unwraps its state refs, similar to a reactive object. `const { user } = useSessionStore()` copies the current user and will not update. `storeToRefs(store)` returns refs for state and getters only. Actions stay methods, so you pull them off the store directly: `const { user } = storeToRefs(store)` and `const { signOut } = store`.

Resetting state is part of the contract. `store.$reset()` exists for options stores. A setup store needs an explicit `$reset` or a `logout()` that replaces every ref, or the next account on a shared browser will see the previous user.
keyPoints: `storeToRefs` is for state and getters. It skips actions.
Do not destructure state directly from the store.
Clear user-specific state on logout.
In tests, create a fresh Pinia with `createPinia()` or the testing helper so stores do not leak between cases.

blocks.title: A setup store and a component that keeps reactivity
blocks.explanation: Components call `useSessionStore()`. They then use `storeToRefs` for `userId` and `signedIn`, and call `store.signOut()` as a method. Replacing `userId` updates every subscriber.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: Why not keep a module-level ref instead of Pinia?
blocks.answer:
A module-level ref works until you need SSR request isolation, devtools, a standard reset, or a plugin. It is also easy to create two "singletons" in tests because the module stays loaded. Pinia gives you one store per app instance, so a test can install a new Pinia and get empty state.

For a tiny widget that no other file reads, the module-level ref is still extra machinery. I introduce a store when a second route or a second unrelated component needs the same state.
blocks.explanation: Pinia's value is lifetime and inspection, not the ability to hold a ref.

blocks.title: storeToRefs on an action
blocks.question: What does `storeToRefs` return for a setup-store action such as `signOut`, and what happens if you call that result from a click handler?
blocks.answer: `storeToRefs` does not wrap actions. Destructuring `signOut` from `storeToRefs(store)` gives `undefined`, so the click throws or no-ops. Take actions from the store object itself. Take state and getters from `storeToRefs`.
blocks.explanation:
The helper exists to preserve reactivity of state. Actions are functions and must keep their store receiver.

[Further reading](https://pinia.vuejs.org/core-concepts/#destructuring-from-a-store)
hints: Which store members are refs?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: An SPA keeps a Pinia cart. After logout, the next user still sees the previous cart until a refresh. SSR tests also fail because a cart id from test A appears in test B. What do you change?
blocks.answer:
`signOut` must reset the cart store as well as the session store, ideally from one place so a new store cannot forget. Prefer a function that walks the user-scoped stores. In tests, create a new Pinia per test or call the reset. On the server, create a new Pinia per request and do not import a store into a module singleton that was created at startup.

Also drop persisted plugins' storage on logout, or the next page load hydrates the old cart from `localStorage`.
blocks.explanation: Shared state needs an explicit end of life. Login boundaries and tests both are ends of life.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Subscribing to the whole store in every row component so a quantity change rerenders the entire catalog.
blocks.whyItHappens: Reading `store.lines` in each row makes every row depend on the array. Any edit replaces or mutates that shared dependency.
blocks.correctApproach: Select the row by id in a computed, keep row components pure where you can, and avoid deep watches of the entire catalog.

blocks.title: Production guidance
blocks.content: Stores hold shared state. Components hold local interaction state.
keyPoints: Use setup stores when you want composable syntax.
Always `storeToRefs` before destructuring state or getters.
Reset user state on logout and isolate Pinia per SSR request and per test.
Cancel or ignore async actions that outlive navigation.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- A Pinia store is a shared composable tied to an app's Pinia instance.
- `storeToRefs` keeps state and getters reactive. It skips actions.
- Direct destructuring copies current values.
- Logout, SSR, and tests all need a fresh or reset store.

Official references

- https://pinia.vuejs.org/core-concepts/
- https://pinia.vuejs.org/core-concepts/#destructuring-from-a-store

title: Async state and cancellation
description: Loading, error, and data flags, plus ignoring stale responses when the user moves on.

blocks.title: Model the request as a small state machine
blocks.content:
A screen that loads data needs more than the payload. Track status (`idle`, `loading`, `success`, `error`), the last error, and the data you are willing to show. Decide whether old data stays visible during a refresh. Checkout often keeps the previous product on screen. A user switch must not keep showing the previous user's orders for even one frame.

Put the transition in one function or composable. If three components each set `loading.value = true` around their own `fetch`, they will clobber each other.
keyPoints: Status and payload are different fields. Empty data and a failed request are different states.
Keep or clear stale data as a product decision, then encode it.
One owner starts the request and applies the result.
Do not store secrets or one user's payload in a module singleton on the server.

blocks.title: Identity decides which response may write
blocks.content:
Every request has an identity: the route param, the query, the account id. When the identity changes, abort the previous `fetch` and ignore its result. `AbortController` is the browser tool. A generation counter works when the API is a callback you cannot abort: increment on start, and write state only if the generation still matches.

Vue does not tie a promise to the component. A promise started in `onMounted` can resolve after unmount. Check an `aborted` flag in `onUnmounted`, or abort the controller there, before assigning to refs. Assigning to a ref after unmount does not resurrect the component, but it can write into a store that is still alive.
keyPoints: Abort on identity change and on unmount.
Ignore `AbortError`. It is cancellation, not a user-facing failure.
A late response must not write if the account or the id has changed.
Suspense in Vue is still an experimental built-in. Do not make a production data layer depend on it becoming the default.

blocks.title: Load a customer and drop stale responses
blocks.explanation: Changing `id` aborts the previous request. A response writes `customer` only if its controller is still current. The `finally` block does not clear `loading` for a request that already lost the race, because the newer request owns that flag.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: How do you stop a slow request for user A from rendering inside user B's session?
blocks.answer:
The request key includes the account id, not only the resource id. On logout or account switch I abort in-flight requests and drop store data before the next user's shell renders. The response handler checks the account id that started the request against the current session and discards mismatches.

I would not rely on route unmount alone. A store survives the component, so a late assignment can repopulate the previous profile.
blocks.explanation: Cancellation has to cover both the component lifetime and the session lifetime.

blocks.title: The finally block that clears the new request
blocks.question: Two watches overlap. Request A fails to check `aborted` in `finally` and sets `loading = false` after request B has already set `loading = true`. What does the screen do?
blocks.answer: The spinner disappears while B is still in flight. A's cleanup ran late and wrote a shared flag. Guard every write, including `finally`, with the same aborted or generation check, or give each request its own state object and point a ref at the latest one.
blocks.explanation:
Shared status flags are state. Stale requests must not assign them.

[Further reading](https://vuejs.org/guide/essentials/watchers.html)
hints: Which request is allowed to assign `loading`?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: A dashboard fires 12 resource requests when a filter changes. Some are cacheable, some must be fresh, and the page unmounts quickly when users switch tabs. How do you structure it?
blocks.answer:
One composable per resource, each keyed by the filter snapshot, each with its own abort. A small cache can keep the last successful payload for a key so returning to a filter feels instant, but the cache key must include the tenant. On unmount, abort the set.

Do not build a single promise that `Promise.all`s every widget if one optional widget failing should not fail the page. Isolate errors per card. Vue's experimental Suspense is not required for that and should not be the backbone.
blocks.explanation: Independent status, a real cache key, and cancellation beat one mega-request.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Setting `data.value = await response.json()` with no check that the component or the id is still current.
blocks.whyItHappens: The happy path is shorter. The bug only appears when responses return out of order.
blocks.correctApproach: Abort, then assign only for the active generation. Cover it with a test that resolves the first request last.

blocks.title: Production guidance
blocks.content: Write the cancellation path before the success path.
keyPoints: Include status, error, and whether stale data remains visible.
Key requests by the identity that must not mix, including the account.
Guard every assignment from an async function.
Treat Suspense as experimental when you design the data layer.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- Loading, error, and data are explicit states.
- Abort or ignore work when the id, the account, or the component changes.
- A late `finally` can corrupt the next request's status.
- Do not depend on experimental Suspense for production loading architecture.

Official references

- https://vuejs.org/guide/essentials/watchers.html
- https://vuejs.org/guide/reusability/composables.html

title: Selecting state management
description: A senior decision framework for local state, provide/inject, Pinia, and the URL.

blocks.title: Put state where its lifetime already exists
blocks.content:
The URL owns state the user can refresh and share: filters, pagination, the open record id. Component state owns hover, an unsent draft, and a disclosure that does not belong in a bookmark. Provide/inject owns a subtree contract such as a form or a menu. A store owns session and cached data that several routes use.

If you cannot name which of those lifetimes you need, do not add a store yet. A store without an owner becomes a global object that every feature imports, and tests start needing the whole application.
keyPoints: Shareable state belongs in the route.
Ephemeral interaction state belongs in the component.
Subtree contracts belong in provide/inject.
Cross-route session state belongs in a store with a reset story.

blocks.title: Server data is not the same as UI state
blocks.content:
A store that copies every API resource "so we have it" becomes a second backend with stale copies. Cache a resource when the product needs instant back-navigation or multiple consumers, and key that cache by tenant and query. Let a screen fetch its own data when it is the only reader and freshness matters more than sharing.

Mutations should describe the user action (`reserveSeat`) rather than `setState(patch)`. The action can update the cache, invalidate a key, or roll back if the request fails.
keyPoints: Do not mirror the entire API in Pinia by default.
Name cache keys with the identity that must not leak across accounts.
Actions beat generic setters at the store boundary.
Optimistic UI needs a rollback path. A watcher that always overwrites from the last response will fight the optimistic value.

blocks.title: Keep the shareable filter in the route
blocks.explanation: Refresh and share keep the filter. The component does not also store a copy in Pinia, so there is one source. Invalid query values fall back to `open`.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: A team asks you to adopt a global store for a new Vue app on day one. What do you say?
blocks.answer:
I ask which state outlives a single page and must be read by unrelated components. The session fits. A modal's open flag and a form draft do not. I would start with component state, the router query for shareable filters, and provide/inject inside a feature subtree. I would add a Pinia store at the first real sharing or caching boundary, with a reset on logout.

Adopting the library early is cheap. Moving every ref into it on day one is what makes the app hard to delete from later.
blocks.explanation: The recommendation is a decision rule, not a ban on Pinia.

blocks.title: Two sources for one filter
blocks.question: The open/closed filter is stored in Pinia and also copied to `route.query` by a deep watch. Users hit Back and the list does not change, or it changes twice. Why?
blocks.answer: Two owners are fighting. Back updates the route, but the store still holds the old filter until a watch runs, and the watch may write the store value back into the route and undo Back. Pick the route as the source and derive the filter with a computed, or pick the store and stop pretending the URL is shareable.
blocks.explanation:
Synchronization watches between two sources of truth create loops and undo navigation.

[Further reading](https://router.vuejs.org/guide/)
hints: Which write runs last, the router or the store watch?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: Product wants a multi-step checkout. Refresh should restore the step only before payment, and the payment step must not be shareable as a URL that skips validation. Where does each piece live?
blocks.answer:
The cart id can be in the session store or in a server session, not only in memory. The step index before payment can be in the URL or in server state if refresh must restore it. The payment confirmation is a server transition: the client sends the request and renders the result. It is not a `?step=pay` link someone can open cold.

Card details stay in the payment component or the payment provider's frame. They do not go into Pinia, the URL, or `localStorage`.
blocks.explanation: Lifetime includes security. Some state should die with the component on purpose.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Dispatching a store action from every presentational component so a button can change a global flag.
blocks.whyItHappens: It avoids prop drilling and also hides the data flow. The button becomes unusable outside that store.
blocks.correctApproach: Emit from the presentational component. Let a container or a feature composable call the store.

blocks.title: Production guidance
blocks.content: Name the owner of each piece of state before choosing a library.
keyPoints: URL for shareable view state.
Component for drafts and ephemeral UI.
Provide/inject for a subtree contract.
Pinia for shared session or cache data that has a reset path.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- Lifetime and audience pick the tool.
- One source of truth. Do not watch a store and the route into each other.
- Server data can stay local to a screen until it is actually shared.
- Secrets and payment details do not belong in global client state.

Official references

- https://pinia.vuejs.org/core-concepts/
- https://router.vuejs.org/guide/

title: Vue Router and lazy routes
description: History modes, route records, params, and what actually creates a lazy chunk.

blocks.title: A route record maps a URL onto components
blocks.content:
Vue Router 4 matches a location against an array of route records. `createWebHistory` uses the HTML5 history API and needs the server to serve the SPA shell for deep links. `createWebHashHistory` keeps the route after `#` and avoids that server rule. `createMemoryHistory` is for tests and for the server, where there is no browser URL bar.

Dynamic segments such as `/users/:id` land in `route.params`. Params are strings, or arrays when the pattern repeats. They are not numbers until you parse them. A component instance is reused when you navigate from `/users/1` to `/users/2` if the same component is matched. `onMounted` does not run again. Watch the param or use `onBeforeRouteUpdate`.
keyPoints: History mode needs a server fallback to `index.html`. Hash mode does not.
Params and query values arrive as strings.
Same-component param changes reuse the instance.
`props: true` on a record passes params in as props, which keeps the page component from depending on the router for every field.

blocks.title: Lazy routes are dynamic imports, not a special component type
blocks.content:
A lazy record uses `component: () => import("./UserPage.vue")`. The function is the chunk boundary. If some eager file also imports `UserPage.vue` statically, the bundler can pull it into the initial graph and the lazy boundary is gone. The same rule applies to stores and helpers that the eager shell imports from a feature folder.

Named chunks and a preview of the network panel are how you verify the split. Adding `defineAsyncComponent` around a route component is usually redundant because the router already loads the import function.
keyPoints: The dynamic `import()` is the split point.
A static import of the same module from the shell defeats it.
Route-level splitting follows features. Component-level async is for heavy widgets inside a page.
Failed chunk loads need an error state. A deploy that deletes old hashed files while a tab is open is a common cause.

blocks.title: Lazy routes and a watched param
blocks.explanation: The page chunk loads when the route is visited. `props: true` passes `id` in, and the watch still covers param changes because the page instance is reused. `loadUser` stands for the cancellable loader from the async-state topic.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: What do you check when a "lazy" route increases the main bundle?
blocks.answer:
I search for static imports of that view, its child components, and any barrel file that re-exports it. I then look at the bundle analyzer to see which chunk contains the module. The router callback can be lazy and still useless if the shell imported the same file for a menu icon map or a unit test helper that ended up in the app graph.

I also check that the server fallback exists for history mode. A bundle split and a refresh 404 are different failures that teams mix up.
blocks.explanation: Lazy is a graph property. The syntax only suggests the boundary.

blocks.title: Param navigation does not remount
blocks.question: `UserPage` loads data inside `onMounted` by reading `route.params.id`. It works for the first user. Clicking a link from `/users/1` to `/users/2` leaves the first user on screen. Why?
blocks.answer: Vue Router reuses the component instance when only params change. `onMounted` does not run for `/users/2`. Watch `() => route.params.id` or use `onBeforeRouteUpdate`, and cancel the request for id 1.
blocks.explanation:
Mount hooks run when the instance is created. A param change is an update of the same instance.

[Further reading](https://router.vuejs.org/guide/)
hints: Does the matched component instance change between those two URLs?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: Marketing wants pretty URLs, engineering wants fewer server changes, and the app is deployed to static file hosting that 404s on `/settings`. What do you recommend?
blocks.answer:
If the host can add a fallback to `index.html`, use `createWebHistory` and add that fallback. If it cannot, `createWebHashHistory` works on static hosting without a server rule, with uglier URLs. Do not switch to history mode and "fix" refresh by making every route a hash anyway.

Document the hosting requirement next to the router setup. It is an operational part of routing, not a component detail.
blocks.explanation: History mode includes the server. The router constructor is only half of it.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Parsing `route.params.id` with `Number` and passing `NaN` into an API call when the segment is missing.
blocks.whyItHappens: TypeScript often types params loosely, and `Number(undefined)` is `NaN` rather than a thrown error.
blocks.correctApproach: Narrow to `string`, validate, and render a not-found state before fetching.

blocks.title: Production guidance
blocks.content: Treat routes as the map of features and of code splitting.
keyPoints: Watch params when the instance is reused.
Keep lazy views out of the eager import graph.
Match history mode to the host's fallback behavior.
Treat params and query as untrusted strings.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- History mode needs a server fallback. Hash mode does not.
- Params are strings. The same component is reused when they change.
- `() => import(...)` defines a lazy route. A static import can erase it.
- `props: true` passes params in as props.

Official references

- https://router.vuejs.org/guide/

title: Navigation guards
description: Global and in-component guards, return values, and why a client guard is not authorization.

blocks.title: Guards decide whether a navigation may finish
blocks.content:
Global `beforeEach` runs for every navigation. Per-route `beforeEnter` runs for that record. `onBeforeRouteLeave` and `onBeforeRouteUpdate` run inside a component. In Vue Router 4 the recommended style is to return `true` or `undefined` to continue, return `false` to cancel, or return a route location to redirect. The older `next` callback still exists. Mixing `next()` and a return value in the same guard is a bug farm. Pick the return style.

Guards can be async. A slow guard leaves the user on the old page until it resolves, so a guard that fetches a large payload is the wrong place for that work. Load data in the page, with its own loading state.
keyPoints: Return a location to redirect. Return `false` to stay.
Do not mix `next()` and return values.
In-component leave guards are the right place for "discard this unsaved draft?"
`beforeEach` is a product policy point. Keep it thin.

blocks.title: Client guards improve UX. The server authorizes.
blocks.content:
A `beforeEach` that checks a Pinia `signedIn` flag can send a stranger to `/login` and can preserve the intended URL. Anyone can edit that flag in devtools or call the API directly. The API must authorize the request. The guard is a convenience.

Do not store access tokens in a place the guard reads from `localStorage` and also log them. Do not trust `route.query.redirect` unless you allow only same-app relative paths. An open redirect is a navigation bug with a security impact.
keyPoints: Guards are not an authorization boundary.
Validate redirect targets as relative paths.
Route meta such as `requiresAuth` should be data the guard interprets, not code pulled from a random component.
Failed chunk loads and cancelled navigations need a path that does not trap the user in a redirect loop.

blocks.title: A thin auth guard with a relative redirect
blocks.explanation: The guard only chooses a screen. `safeRedirect` refuses protocol-relative URLs. The API still checks the session on every request.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: Where should an unsaved-changes prompt live?
blocks.answer:
In `onBeforeRouteLeave` on the page that owns the draft, or in a composable that page calls. The guard asks only when the draft is dirty and returns `false` if the user chooses to stay. A global guard that inspects every store for a `dirty` flag becomes a registry of features and is easy to forget to clear.

Browser refresh is a different event. `beforeRouteLeave` does not run for a tab close. Use `beforeunload` only when losing the draft is expensive, and do not rely on a custom modal there. Browsers show their own dialog.
blocks.explanation: Leave guards cover in-app navigation. They are not a substitute for persistence or for `beforeunload`.

blocks.title: The redirect loop
blocks.question: Login has `meta.requiresAuth: true` by accident, and the guard redirects unauthenticated users to `{ name: "login" }`. What happens when a signed-out user opens `/login`?
blocks.answer: The guard redirects to login, which triggers the guard again, forever. Auth meta does not belong on the login route. The guard should also bail out when `to.name` is already the login route before returning a redirect.
blocks.explanation:
A redirect is a new navigation. The guard runs again on the target.

[Further reading](https://router.vuejs.org/guide/advanced/navigation-guards.html)
hints: Which route is the guard sending the user toward, and does that route match the same rule?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: Editors have a profile form, a separate roles screen, and a global guard that tries to block navigation whenever any form store is dirty. People get stuck on the roles screen after a successful save. How do you untangle it?
blocks.answer:
Remove the global dirty check. Each editor page registers its own leave guard and clears its dirty flag when the save promise resolves, before it navigates. The roles screen does not read the profile form store.

If product wants one prompt for the whole settings area, the settings parent route owns one draft coordinator. Child routes do not each invent a flag. The coordinator resets on save and on leaving `/settings`.
blocks.explanation: Dirty state should be owned by the same feature that can clear it.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Calling `next()` and also returning a route location from the same guard.
blocks.whyItHappens: Examples from different Vue Router versions got copied together. The navigation resolves twice or warns and cancels.
blocks.correctApproach: Use return values only, unless the codebase has a documented `next` convention and you follow it exclusively.

blocks.title: Production guidance
blocks.content: Keep global guards small, pure, and loop-free.
keyPoints: Authorize on the server. Use guards to pick a screen.
Allow only relative redirect targets.
Put unsaved prompts on the page that owns the draft.
Test the login route and a deep link separately.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- Return `false`, `true`, or a location. Do not mix in `next()`.
- Param updates can use `onBeforeRouteUpdate` instead of remounting.
- Client guards are UX. APIs authorize.
- A redirect target that matches the same guard is a loop.

Official references

- https://router.vuejs.org/guide/advanced/navigation-guards.html

title: Form architecture
description: Controlled fields, drafts, validation timing, and native form submit.

blocks.title: One draft, one submit path
blocks.content:
A form component owns a draft object. Fields bind to that draft with `v-model`. The parent passes initial values as props and receives the submitted value through an event. That is easier to test than a page that reads ten inputs through template refs.

Use a native `<form @submit.prevent="onSubmit">` so Enter works and password managers recognize the form. The `.prevent` modifier stops the browser navigation. Disable the submit button while a request is in flight, but do not disable the whole form before you have copied the values you need, or you can drop fields from the payload.
keyPoints: Bind fields to a draft. Emit the draft on submit.
Use a real form element and prevent the browser submit.
Do not mutate the prop that seeded the draft.
Reset the draft from the prop only when you mean to discard edits.

blocks.title: Validate for the moment the user is in
blocks.content:
Validating every keystroke on a pristine field shows errors before the user has finished. A practical policy is: validate a field on blur, re-validate on input after the first error, and validate the whole form on submit. The error message sits next to the control and is linked with `aria-describedby`.

Schema libraries are optional. The important part is a pure function from draft to error map so the same rules run in a unit test without mounting the page. Async rules, such as "username taken", need cancellation when the draft changes.
keyPoints: Pure validation functions are easier than rules hidden in watchers.
Show errors after blur or submit, then keep them current.
Server errors map onto fields by a stable code, not by English sentence matching.
Client validation is a hint. The server validates again.

blocks.title: A draft that commits on submit
blocks.explanation: The prop seeds the draft once. Later typing stays local until submit. The parent hears one `save` event with the trimmed value.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: How do you handle a form whose initial values arrive after the component has mounted?
blocks.answer:
Do not assume props exist in setup. Either wait to render the form until the request succeeds (`v-if="user"` so the form mounts with real initial data), or copy props into the draft in a watch that runs only while the draft is clean. Mounting the form after data arrives is the simpler reset policy.

If the user has started typing and the server pushes a newer profile, do not clobber the draft. Show a "this record changed" prompt.
blocks.explanation: Initialization timing is a product rule. `v-if` remount gives you a clean start.

blocks.title: Disabled fields dropped from the payload
blocks.question: A submit handler builds the payload with `new FormData(event.currentTarget)`. A field was disabled because the user lacks permission. Why is it missing, and is that a problem?
blocks.answer: The browser omits disabled fields from form submission. That is a problem if the handler assumed FormData was the full draft. Read the draft object instead, and let the server ignore fields the user cannot edit. Disabling is a UI hint, not the authorization check.
blocks.explanation:
FormData follows HTML rules. A reactive draft follows your state. Pick one and test it.

[Further reading](https://vuejs.org/guide/essentials/forms.html)
hints: What does the browser include in a native form submission?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: A settings form has 60 fields across tabs, and saving tab A loses in-progress edits on tab B because each tab fetches and replaces a shared reactive object. How do you restructure it?
blocks.answer:
One draft for the whole settings document, created when the document loads. Tabs are views over slices of that draft, not separate fetchers. Save sends the whole draft or a patch computed from the original. A tab change must not replace the draft.

If the document is large enough that teams own sections, give each section its own draft and its own save endpoint, and stop sharing one reactive object. Do not mix those two models in one object.
blocks.explanation: Tabs are navigation inside one draft unless the API really saves sections independently.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Using `watch(draft, save, { deep: true })` to autosave on every keystroke.
blocks.whyItHappens: It skips the submit event and races with validation. Failed requests leave the user with no idea which version was stored.
blocks.correctApproach: Autosave on a debounce of a serialized clean snapshot, show the save status, and ignore responses that are older than the latest snapshot.

blocks.title: Production guidance
blocks.content: Make the draft explicit and the validation pure.
keyPoints: Seed from props once, or mount the form only after data is ready.
Validate on blur and submit, then on input after an error.
Map server field errors back by code.
Keep authorization on the server even if the control is disabled.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- A draft plus a submit event is the basic Vue form.
- Use a native form with `@submit.prevent`.
- Disabled inputs are omitted from `FormData`.
- Do not replace a shared draft just because a tab changed.

Official references

- https://vuejs.org/guide/essentials/forms.html
- https://vuejs.org/guide/components/v-model.html

title: Metadata-driven forms
description: Rendering fields from a schema without losing accessibility or type safety.

blocks.title: The schema is data. The renderer is a small interpreter.
blocks.content:
Admin tools and workflow products often describe fields as JSON: type, label, required, options. A renderer walks that list and mounts a known set of controls. The schema should name a field type you implement (`text`, `money`, `select`), not a random component path from the network. Loading a component by a URL stored in the schema is an XSS and supply-chain hole.

Each field still needs a stable `name`, a label, and an error id. Generate ids with `useId()` per field component so two schemas on one page do not collide.
keyPoints: Map a closed set of field types to components you wrote.
Do not `import()` a path that came from the server.
Keys for `v-for` are field names, not array indexes, when names are stable.
Unknown field types render a visible unsupported state, not a silent skip, in authoring tools.

blocks.title: Validation lives next to the schema, not in each screen
blocks.content:
If every screen reimplements "required" by hand, the renderer was not worth it. The schema carries constraints and one validator interprets them. Field components emit `update:modelValue`. They do not each POST to the API.

Conditional fields (`show when country is US`) belong in the schema as expressions over the draft, evaluated by your code. Evaluating a server-provided string with `new Function` is code injection. Use a small explicit operator set (`equals`, `in`).
keyPoints: One validator reads the schema and the draft.
Conditions are data, not JavaScript strings.
Hidden fields need a defined policy: omit them from the payload or submit their last value.
Changing the schema while a user is mid-form needs a migration of the draft, not a hot reload of types under their cursor.

blocks.title: Render a closed set of field types
blocks.explanation: The renderer looks up a component from a local map. A schema type that is not in the map never becomes a dynamic import. The template uses `<component :is="components[field.type]">` with `:key="field.name"`.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: What do you refuse to put in a JSON form schema?
blocks.answer:
Arbitrary JavaScript, HTML for labels that authors treat as trusted when they are not, component URLs, and CSS from the schema that lands in a style attribute without sanitizing. I also refuse to let the schema name a Pinia store or an API endpoint per field. The host screen owns submission. The schema owns field structure and constraints.

Rich text is the usual exception that needs a sanitizer and an explicit field type, not a generic `html` type.
blocks.explanation: A schema interpreter is safe when the instruction set is closed.

blocks.title: Index keys reset the wrong field
blocks.question: Fields are rendered with `:key="index"`. The user types in the second field, then a condition inserts a new field at the top. Where does the typed text go?
blocks.answer: Vue reuses the component instance that had key `1` for different schema rows, so the typed state can stick to the wrong field or be destroyed. Key by `field.name`. If names can be duplicated, the schema is invalid and should be rejected when it is saved.
blocks.explanation:
Dynamic forms reorder. Index keys attach local input state to a position.

[Further reading](https://vuejs.org/guide/essentials/list.html)
hints: What does Vue reuse when the key stays the same and the item at that index changes?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: An enterprise form builder lets staff add fields. Some fields are only valid for a country. Submissions for hidden fields are inconsistent. How do you specify the behavior?
blocks.answer:
Write the rule down: when a field becomes hidden, its draft value is retained in the editor but omitted from the submit payload, and it is cleared when the user saves successfully. Validation does not flag hidden fields. The server applies the same omit rule so a hand-crafted request cannot set a hidden field either.

Test a case that hides a required field and submits. The client and the server should both accept it.
blocks.explanation: Hidden-field policy is part of the schema semantics and has to match on the server.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Binding `:is="field.component"` where `component` is a string path from the API.
blocks.whyItHappens: It is the most direct reading of "dynamic". It lets the API choose code.
blocks.correctApproach: Look up a component in a local map. Ignore unknown types safely.

blocks.title: Production guidance
blocks.content: Keep the schema language smaller than JavaScript.
keyPoints: Closed field-type map.
Stable keys and `useId` labels.
One validator shared with tests.
The same visibility and omit rules on the server.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- Render a closed set of components from schema data.
- Do not evaluate schema strings as code.
- Key fields by name.
- Define what happens to hidden values, then test the server too.

Official references

- https://vuejs.org/guide/essentials/forms.html
- https://vuejs.org/guide/essentials/list.html

title: List identity and keys
description: How Vue reuses DOM nodes, why index keys corrupt state, and what a key does not do.

blocks.title: The key tells Vue which node is the same item
blocks.content:
When a `v-for` list updates, Vue matches old and new children by key. A stable id lets Vue move the existing DOM node and component instance. The default, if you omit the key, is like matching by position. An explicit index key does the same thing and also blocks Vue from warning you.

Local state inside a row, such as an input or a child's `ref`, stays with the component instance. If the key changes, Vue destroys that instance and creates another. That is useful when you want a reset. It is a bug when a sort destroys inputs because the keys were indexes.
keyPoints: Key by a stable id from the data.
Index keys break as soon as the list reorders, is filtered, or is prepended.
Changing the key on purpose remounts the subtree.
The key goes on the element or component that `v-for` creates, not on a wrapper that never moves.

blocks.title: Keys do not virtualize and do not stop parent renders
blocks.content:
A correct key avoids mismatched state. It does not skip rendering 10,000 rows. The parent that owns the `v-for` still creates vnode children for each item. If the parent rerenders, those vnodes are diffed. Cheap row props and computed slices reduce the work. Windowing reduces the DOM.

`v-memo` can skip updating a subtree when the values in its array are unchanged. It is a precision tool for expensive rows, not a default on every `v-for`. A wrong memo dependency serves stale UI, which is worse than a slow row.
keyPoints: Keys preserve identity. They are not a performance budget.
Filter before rendering, in a computed.
`v-memo` dependencies must include every value the row displays.
TransitionGroup also requires keys, because it tracks entering and leaving nodes.

blocks.title: Stable keys after a sort
blocks.code:
<script setup lang="ts">
import { computed, ref } from 'vue'

const props = defineProps<{ rows: { id: string; label: string }[] }>()
const direction = ref<'asc' | 'desc'>('asc')
const ordered = computed(() => {
  const copy = props.rows.slice()
  copy.sort((a, b) => a.label.localeCompare(b.label))
  return direction.value === 'asc' ? copy : copy.reverse()
})
</script>

<template>
  <article v-for="row in ordered" :key="row.id">
    <RowEditor :label="row.label" />
  </article>
</template>
blocks.explanation: Sorting creates a new order, but each `RowEditor` keeps its instance because `row.id` did not change. An index key would hand the editor to a different row.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: When would you change a key to force a remount?
blocks.answer:
When the instance's local state must not survive a logical identity change. A player component keyed by `track.id` remounts when the track changes and drops the previous audio node. A form keyed by `record.id` starts empty fields instead of showing the previous record's draft.

I would not change the key on every parent render, and I would not use a random number. The key should be the identity whose change means "this is a different thing".
blocks.explanation: Remounting is a feature when identity changes and a bug when identity is stable.

blocks.title: Index keys and prepend
blocks.question: A todo list uses `:key="index"`. Each row has an input bound to local state. The user types in the first row, then a new todo is inserted at index 0. What happens to the typed text?
blocks.answer: The text stays on the component whose key is still `0`, which is now the new todo's position, or the instances shift in a way that shows the draft on the wrong row. The data array and the input state disagree. Key by `todo.id`.
blocks.explanation:
Index keys mean "same position", not "same todo".

[Further reading](https://vuejs.org/guide/essentials/list.html)
hints: Which instance does Vue keep when the item at key 0 is a different todo?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: A realtime table updates 200 rows a second and also lets people expand a row locally. Expanded state resets whenever any row ticks. How do you separate those updates?
blocks.answer:
Key rows by id so expansion state lives on a stable component, or lift expansion into a set of ids in the parent so it does not depend on instance identity. Stop rerendering every row when one price changes: pass a single row object from a map keyed by id, and make the row a component whose other props are stable.

If the DOM is still too big, window it. Do not `v-memo` the expanded row's open flag out of the dependency list.
blocks.explanation: Identity, update granularity, and DOM size are three levers.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Using the entire object as a key via `:key="row"` in the template without a stable primitive.
blocks.whyItHappens: Vue will stringify or diff in a way that changes when the parent replaces the object with an equal copy, remounting rows on every fetch.
blocks.correctApproach: Key by `row.id`. Replace objects freely.

blocks.title: Production guidance
blocks.content: Choose the key from the domain id, then measure whether the list is still too big.
keyPoints: Never use the index for a reorderable or filterable list.
Change the key when you intend to reset local state.
Memo only expensive rows, with complete dependencies.
Virtualize before micro-optimizing the diff.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- Keys identify nodes across updates.
- Index keys attach local state to a position.
- A new key remounts. A stable key preserves instance state.
- Keys do not window the DOM.

Official references

- https://vuejs.org/guide/essentials/list.html
- https://vuejs.org/guide/extras/rendering-mechanism.html

title: Render cost
description: What makes a Vue component re-render, and which optimizations are worth it.

blocks.title: A component re-renders when its reactive reads change
blocks.content:
Vue 3 tracks effects at the property level. A component re-renders when a ref it read during render changes, when a reactive property it read changes, or when a parent passes a prop whose value changed. Unlike a naive "parent rendered, so children render" model, a child that received the same props and reads no changed state can skip its update. That skip fails if the parent passes a fresh object or inline arrow function every time, because the prop value is a new identity even when the contents look equal.

Computed caches help only when the same computed is read. Creating `computed(() => ...)` inside the render path creates a new computed every time and caches nothing useful. Create it once in setup.
keyPoints: Stable primitive props are cheap to compare.
Fresh object and function props look like changes.
Create computeds and event handlers in setup, or accept that a new function is a new prop.
A child that reads a store directly rerenders when that store field changes, even if the parent did not pass it.

blocks.title: Measure before v-memo and manual caches
blocks.content:
The Vue devtools performance timeline and the browser performance panel tell you whether the cost is script, style, or layout. `v-once` freezes a subtree. `v-memo="[a, b]"` skips the update when `a` and `b` are unchanged. Both can serve stale UI if a dependency is missing. They are appropriate for a proven hot row, not as a default style.

Large lists need fewer DOM nodes, not a faster diff of all of them. A windowing approach renders the viewport. Charts should update through their own API in a watcher, not through Vue recreating a canvas every tick.
keyPoints: Profile script time and layout time separately.
`v-memo` dependencies are an allowlist. Omissions are stale UI.
Do not deep-watch a large list to "be safe".
Move work that does not affect the screen out of the render path.

blocks.title: Stable handlers and primitive props
blocks.code:
<script setup lang="ts">
const props = defineProps<{ rows: { id: string; label: string; cents: number }[] }>()
const emit = defineEmits<{ select: [id: string] }>()

function select(id: string) {
  emit('select', id)
}
</script>

<template>
  <RowItem
    v-for="row in rows"
    :key="row.id"
    :label="row.label"
    :cents="row.cents"
    @select="select(row.id)"
  />
</template>
blocks.explanation: The template still creates a small wrapper per row. The expensive part, `RowItem`, receives primitives. If a profile shows the inline listener defeating a skip, move the id into the row component and emit from there so the parent passes one stable function created in setup.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: A parent rerenders every second because of a clock, and a heavy list underneath janks. What do you check first?
blocks.answer:
I check whether the list is in the same component as the clock. If it is, split the clock into a child so the list component does not re-render every tick. If they are already split, I check whether the parent passes a new array or a new style object into the list each time. Then I profile one row. I add `v-memo` only if a row is expensive and its inputs are easy to list.

I would not freeze the clock with `v-once`. The clock is supposed to change. The list is not supposed to care.
blocks.explanation: Isolate the fast-changing read from the expensive tree before reaching for memoization.

blocks.title: A new object prop every render
blocks.question:
Why does `RowItem` update on every parent render here?

`<RowItem :style="{ color: row.color }" />`

`row.color` did not change.
blocks.answer: The template literal object is a new object every time the parent renders. The `style` prop identity changes, so the child updates. Pass `row.color` as a string prop and set the style inside `RowItem`, or compute a stable style object when the color changes.
blocks.explanation:
Vue compares the prop value you passed. It does not deep-compare a fresh object for you.

[Further reading](https://vuejs.org/guide/best-practices/performance.html)
hints: Is the style object the same reference as last render?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: Switching a dashboard filter re-renders 800 cards and drops frames, but each card's data is a primitive. The filter is local to the toolbar. What is the likely coupling?
blocks.answer: The toolbar and the grid share a component, so the filter keystroke rerenders the grid, or each card reads the filter store directly. Split the toolbar. Make cards depend only on their row id and a selected id. If all 800 cards are in the DOM, virtualize them. Confirm with a performance trace that the time is in Vue patch or in layout, and fix that layer.
blocks.explanation: Primitive props do not help if the component that renders the `v-for` is the one receiving the keystrokes.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Wrapping every child in `v-memo` with an empty array to "stop renders".
blocks.whyItHappens: An empty dependency list never updates the subtree, so the UI goes stale and the team adds more force-update hacks.
blocks.correctApproach: Isolate state first. Memo a row only with the values it actually displays, after a profile shows the row is expensive.

blocks.title: Production guidance
blocks.content: Reduce how often the expensive component is asked to render, then reduce how much DOM it builds.
keyPoints: Split fast-changing state into its own component.
Pass stable primitives into rows.
Create computeds in setup, not in the template.
Virtualize long lists before micro-optimizing the patch.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- Components update when the reactive values they read change.
- New object and function identities count as changes.
- `v-memo` and `v-once` can freeze stale UI.
- Long lists need fewer DOM nodes.

Official references

- https://vuejs.org/guide/best-practices/performance.html
- https://vuejs.org/guide/extras/rendering-mechanism.html

title: Async components
description: defineAsyncComponent, loading and error states, and how this differs from a lazy route.

blocks.title: Async components load a chunk when they are rendered
blocks.content:
`defineAsyncComponent(() => import("./Chart.vue"))` returns a component wrapper. Vue calls the loader when the wrapper is first rendered, not when the module is defined. That is useful for a heavy editor or chart inside a tab that many users never open. A route-level `() => import()` is still the right split for an entire page, because the router owns the loading of that page.

The options form can show a loading component after a delay, show an error component, and set a timeout. The delay avoids a spinner flash on a fast network. The timeout is a product decision: a chunk that never arrives should not spin forever.
keyPoints: The loader runs on render, which creates the chunk boundary.
A static import of the same file elsewhere removes the benefit.
Loading and error components should be small and already in the parent chunk.
Vue Suspense can coordinate async setup, and it is still experimental. Prefer an explicit loading prop or the async component options for production screens.

blocks.title: Failure and retry are part of the API
blocks.content:
Chunk load failures happen during deploys when an open tab asks for a hashed file that the new deploy deleted. The error component should offer a reload, not a blank card. Retrying the import function once is reasonable. Retrying forever hides an outage.

Do not fetch the user's data inside the async component's loader. The loader's job is to download code. The component's setup fetches data, with the cancellation rules from the async-state topic. Mixing them makes the loading spinner mean two different things.
keyPoints: Separate code loading from data loading.
Offer a reload when a chunk 404s after a deploy.
Reset a failed async subtree with a key if the user retries.
Timeouts should surface an error state.

blocks.title: A chart panel that loads on first use
blocks.code:
import { defineAsyncComponent } from 'vue'
import LoadError from './LoadError.vue'
import Spinner from './Spinner.vue'

export const ChartPanel = defineAsyncComponent({
  loader: () => import('./ChartPanel.vue'),
  loadingComponent: Spinner,
  errorComponent: LoadError,
  delay: 200,
  timeout: 10000,
})
blocks.explanation: The spinner appears only if the chunk takes longer than 200 ms. After 10 seconds the error component renders. `ChartPanel.vue` itself is responsible for loading data once the code has arrived.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: How do you decide between a lazy route and an async component?
blocks.answer:
If the user navigated to a different page, split at the route so the page's code is not in the first bundle. If the user is already on the page and a heavy widget might never be shown, split that widget with `defineAsyncComponent` or a dynamic import inside `v-if`. Doing both is fine when the page is lazy and it still contains a rare chart.

I would not async-wrap every component. Each split has a request and a loading state. Tiny components belong next to their parent.
blocks.explanation: Split along user-visible boundaries, not along every file.

blocks.title: The eager static import
blocks.question: A route is lazy, and the route file contains `import ChartPanel from "./ChartPanel.vue"` plus a separate `defineAsyncComponent(() => import("./ChartPanel.vue"))`. Why is the chart still in the route chunk?
blocks.answer: The static import already pulled `ChartPanel.vue` into the route chunk. The async wrapper loads a module that is already there. Remove the static import and render only the async component.
blocks.explanation:
A dynamic import is not a split if the same module is also imported statically from a loaded file.

[Further reading](https://vuejs.org/guide/components/async.html)
hints: Which import does the bundler treat as a reason to include the module now?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: After each Friday deploy, users who left a tab open see blank charts until they refresh. How do you handle it?
blocks.answer:
The chart's error component detects a failed dynamic import and tells the user the app updated, with a button that calls `location.reload()`. Optionally, listen for the deploy through your own version endpoint and prompt before the chunk fails. Do not silently retry for minutes.

Keep the loading component in the already-loaded bundle so the failure UI itself does not depend on the missing chunk.
blocks.explanation: Hashed assets and long-lived tabs are an expected production case.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Using experimental Suspense as the only loading UI around every data fetch.
blocks.whyItHappens: The API looks like the async-component solution. Its stability warning is easy to skip, and error handling differs from a normal request.
blocks.correctApproach: Use async components for code. Use explicit status fields for data. Revisit Suspense if Vue marks it stable and the behavior matches your error UX.

blocks.title: Production guidance
blocks.content: Split rare, heavy UI. Keep the fallback local and the error recoverable.
keyPoints: Prefer route splits for pages and async components for heavy optional widgets.
Set a delay and a timeout.
Do not static-import the lazy module.
Plan for a missing chunk after deploy.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- `defineAsyncComponent` loads code when the component is rendered.
- A static import defeats the split.
- Loading UI and data fetching are different stages.
- Suspense is experimental. Chunk errors need a reload path.

Official references

- https://vuejs.org/guide/components/async.html

title: Large dashboard updates
description: How to apply a fast stream of updates without rerendering every widget.

blocks.title: Ingest once, publish narrow slices
blocks.content:
A dashboard that opens a WebSocket in every card multiplies connections and parses the same payload many times. One subscriber should read the stream, normalize it into a map of id to row, and let each card read its id. Batch messages for a frame or two with `requestAnimationFrame` or a short timer so 50 messages become one Vue update.

Store the map in a `shallowRef`. On each batch, copy the map, replace the rows that changed, and assign it once. A card's computed finds its row. If assigning the whole map still invalidates every card, give hot rows their own `shallowRef` so a price change notifies one computed.
keyPoints: One connection and one parser.
Batch before touching Vue state.
Cards read by id. They do not filter the full array.
Charts take data through their API. Do not remount the chart component to change a series.

blocks.title: The DOM and the canvas have their own budgets
blocks.content:
Vue finishing a patch in 5 ms does not matter if 300 charts repaint. Update a chart instance in place from a watcher that reads one row. Mark the instance `markRaw`. Virtualize or unmount cards that are off-screen. `v-show` keeps canvases alive and painting if you are not careful. `v-if` or an intersection observer should stop work that the user cannot see.

Measure on the hardware you claim to support. Record long tasks, dropped frames, and the heap after an hour so a leaked chart instance is visible.
keyPoints: Separate parse time, Vue patch time, and paint time.
Off-screen widgets should not keep animating.
Stable component keys so a batch does not remount cards.
Backpressure: if the socket outruns the UI, drop intermediate frames and show the latest.

blocks.title: Batch socket rows into one shallow map
blocks.explanation: Many socket events collapse into one map assignment per frame. Each card computes only its id. The map is shallow, so Vue is not proxying every cell.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: What do you optimize first when 300 cards all listen to one bus?
blocks.answer:
I remove the duplicate subscriptions and the duplicate parsing before I tune Vue. Then I batch and publish by id. Then I check whether the cards are in the DOM and whether charts repaint. A computed or a memoization tweak is not the first step if the page opened 300 sockets or rebuilt a full array of objects per message.

I would state a budget: one socket, at most one Vue commit per frame, and no canvas work for hidden cards.
blocks.explanation: The first win is usually fewer owners of the stream, not a faster component.

blocks.title: A computed that still reruns every card
blocks.question: Each card does `computed(() => [...map.value.values()].find((row) => row.id === id))`. The map is a shallowRef and you assign it once per frame. Why do all cards still do work proportional to the map size?
blocks.answer: Every card reads the whole map and copies it into an array before finding one id. Any assignment invalidates every computed, and each one walks every row. Read `map.value.get(id)` so the work per card is a lookup. If that is still too broad because every card read the same shallow ref, split hot rows into their own refs.
blocks.explanation:
A shallow ref assignment wakes every computed that read it. The computed should not turn that into an O(n) scan.

[Further reading](https://vuejs.org/guide/best-practices/performance.html)
hints: Which data does each computed read before it finds its row?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: Traders leave the dashboard open all day. Memory climbs until the tab crashes. The Vue update rate looks fine. Where do you look?
blocks.answer:
Look for chart instances that were not destroyed on route change or when a card left the window, socket handlers registered per card, and arrays that append history without a cap. Take a heap snapshot after opening and closing the route twice. The retained objects are usually the library instance and its canvas, held by a module-level cache or by a watcher that never stopped.

Cap series length. Disconnect observers and sockets in `onUnmounted`. Recreate a chart only when its identity changes, not on every price.
blocks.explanation: A smooth patch can still leak if the imperative libraries outlive the components.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Replacing the entire dashboard array and keying rows by index so Vue remounts every chart per batch.
blocks.whyItHappens: It is the shortest way to "refresh the data". Remounting reinitializes canvases and drops local UI state.
blocks.correctApproach: Update by id, keep stable keys, and push data into existing chart instances.

blocks.title: Production guidance
blocks.content: Budget the stream, the Vue commit, and the paint separately.
keyPoints: Ingest once and batch to a frame.
Publish by id with a shallow structure.
Keep foreign instances `markRaw` and update them in place.
Unload off-screen work and prove the heap is stable.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- One subscriber batches updates and writes a map.
- Cards select by id. They do not scan the full list.
- Charts update in place and are destroyed with the card.
- Hidden cards should stop painting.

Official references

- https://vuejs.org/guide/best-practices/performance.html
- https://vuejs.org/guide/extras/reactivity-in-depth.html

title: Vapor Mode
description: What the Vue 3.6 release candidate changes, and what it deliberately does not run.

blocks.title: Vapor Mode is an opt-in compiler, not the Vue 3.5 default
blocks.content:
As of 20 November 2026, the stable Vue release is 3.5.x and Vue 3.6 is a release candidate. Vapor Mode is the headline of that 3.6 line. It compiles single-file components to an update strategy that does not build a VDOM for that component, with the goal of less baseline JavaScript and Solid-like update performance. You opt in with `<script setup vapor>` or `<template vapor>`. Existing VDOM components stay as they are.

The Vue team describes Vapor as feature-complete in the 3.6 RC and recommends it for performance-sensitive pages inside an existing app, or for small new apps, not as a blind rewrite of a large production system.
keyPoints: Stable production apps stay on Vue 3.5 unless they choose to adopt the 3.6 RC knowingly.
Vapor is opt-in per component. It is not a global flag that recompiles the Options API.
A pure Vapor app can use `createVaporApp()` and skip shipping the VDOM runtime.
Mixing Vapor and VDOM requires `vaporInteropPlugin`, which pulls the VDOM runtime back in.

blocks.title: Several Vue features are outside the Vapor subset
blocks.content:
Vapor Mode does not support the Options API. `getCurrentInstance()` returns null in a Vapor component. `app.config.globalProperties` is not available. `v-memo` does not apply. Component template refs do not expose `$el`, `$props`, `$attrs`, `$slots`, or `$refs`. Custom directives use a different interface. `@vue:*` per-element lifecycle events are not supported.

Vapor delegates eligible native events to `document`. Code that depends on `stopPropagation()` meaning the same thing as in a VDOM listener needs a dedicated test. The practical migration is a leaf widget with a performance trace, behind the interop plugin if the rest of the app is still VDOM, not a repo-wide codemod.
keyPoints: Do not put Vapor on an Options API component and expect it to compile.
Avoid deep Vapor/VDOM nesting. Keep a boundary between regions.
Interop is for props, events, and slots, and the RC notes say edge cases remain.
Judge Vapor with a trace of the hot component, not with a blanket claim that Vue got faster.

blocks.title: Opt in on one component
blocks.code:
<script setup vapor lang="ts">
import { ref } from 'vue'

const count = ref(0)
</script>

<template>
  <button type="button" @click="count++">{{ count }}</button>
</template>
blocks.explanation: The `vapor` attribute selects the Vapor compiler for this SFC only. The rest of a Vue 3.5 VDOM app does not become Vapor. Shipping this requires a Vue 3.6 RC or later toolchain, which is not the current stable default.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: Would you turn on Vapor Mode for an entire production app today?
blocks.answer:
No. I would stay on the stable 3.5 line for the application default. If a measured screen is limited by VDOM update cost, I would prototype that screen as a Vapor component on the 3.6 RC, with the interop plugin if it must live inside the existing tree, and I would retest directives, events, and template refs because those APIs differ.

I would also keep a rollback that is just "this component compiles as VDOM again". A rewrite that depends on `globalProperties` or the Options API is not a Vapor candidate.
blocks.explanation: The senior answer separates the stable default from a measured opt-in experiment.

blocks.title: getCurrentInstance in a Vapor component
blocks.question: A composable calls `getCurrentInstance()` to read `proxy.$route`, and it works in a normal Vue 3.5 component. Why does it break after the SFC is marked `vapor`?
blocks.answer: In a Vapor component `getCurrentInstance()` returns null. Vapor does not expose the VDOM component proxy, and `globalProperties` such as a `$route` attached that way are outside the supported subset. Inject the router with `useRoute()` from Vue Router, which uses provide/inject, or keep this component on the VDOM compiler.
blocks.explanation:
Vapor drops APIs that depend on the component proxy. Composables that peeked at the instance need a real injection.

[Further reading](https://github.com/vuejs/core/releases/tag/v3.6.0-rc.1)
hints: What does Vapor return from `getCurrentInstance()`?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: A list of 5,000 live prices is the slowest page in a Vue 3.5 app. Leadership wants Vapor Mode scheduled as the fix. How do you respond?
blocks.answer:
I profile first. If the time is in network parsing, chart paint, or rendering 5,000 DOM nodes, Vapor will not remove that work. Window the list and publish by id. If the trace shows VDOM patch cost on a small DOM, a Vapor pilot of that list component is justified on a branch, with a rollback to the VDOM file.

I would not block the performance fix on a release candidate, and I would not convert the settings pages in the same project.
blocks.explanation: Vapor is a compiler strategy for a measured hot component. It is not the first answer to a large DOM.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Assuming `<script setup vapor>` on one child speeds up its VDOM parent for free.
blocks.whyItHappens: The attribute looks global. The parent still renders VDOM, and interop has a cost at the boundary.
blocks.correctApproach: Put the hot leaf in Vapor, keep a simple boundary, and compare traces before and after.

blocks.title: Production guidance
blocks.content: Treat Vapor as an opt-in RC feature with an explicit subset.
keyPoints: Ship the app on stable Vue 3.5 unless a pilot says otherwise.
Read the unsupported list before converting a component: Options API, instance proxy, `v-memo`, global properties.
Use `createVaporApp` only when the app is actually Vapor end to end.
Keep a VDOM fallback for the piloted component.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- Vue 3.5 is the stable line. Vapor arrives with the Vue 3.6 release candidate.
- Opt in per SFC with `vapor`. It is not the Options API.
- `getCurrentInstance()` is null and VDOM instance fields are absent.
- Pilot a measured leaf. Do not convert the app by default.

Official references

- https://github.com/vuejs/core/releases/tag/v3.6.0-rc.1

title: Vite and bundle boundaries
description: How the Vue plugin, env variables, and dynamic imports decide what ships to the browser.

blocks.title: Vite compiles SFCs and code-splits on dynamic import
blocks.content:
A Vue app on Vite uses `@vitejs/plugin-vue` to compile single-file components. Dev mode serves native ESM and is fast because it does not bundle the whole app first. Production `vite build` rolls modules into chunks. The split points are dynamic `import()` calls: lazy routes, async components, and any other dynamic import you wrote.

Barrel files that re-export every feature pull those features into whoever imported the barrel. A menu that imports `src/features/index.ts` can undo a morning of route-level splitting. Prefer direct file imports at feature boundaries.
keyPoints: Dev ESM behavior is not the production chunk graph. Inspect the build.
Dynamic import defines a split. A static import from an already loaded file removes it.
Barrel files hide static imports.
Sourcemaps and a bundle visualizer are how you check the claim, not the router syntax alone.

blocks.title: VITE_ variables are public
blocks.content:
Only variables prefixed with `VITE_` are exposed to client code, through `import.meta.env`. Vite inlines them into the bundle at build time. Anyone who can load the JavaScript can read them. API base URLs belong there. Secret keys, database passwords, and private tokens do not. A secret the browser must not see stays on the server.

`import.meta.env.DEV` and `PROD` are build modes. Do not hide a security check behind `DEV`. The production bundle will not contain the dev branch, but attackers do not need your dev bundle if the API itself is open.
keyPoints: If it is in client code, it is public, including `VITE_` values.
Inlining happens at build time. Changing the host env after deploy does not change an already built SPA unless you rebuild.
Do not use different API authorization rules in dev and prod.
Preview the production build before judging chunk size. The dev server is not that build.

blocks.title: Read a public API base URL
blocks.explanation: The base URL is public configuration. The throw fails the build or the boot when it is missing, instead of calling `undefined/api`. The token that authorizes the request is not read from `import.meta.env`.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: Someone suggests putting a third-party secret in `VITE_PRIVATE_KEY` so the client can call the vendor directly. What do you say?
blocks.answer:
The value will be in the JavaScript sent to every visitor. I would put the secret on a server or a serverless function that holds it and calls the vendor. The client calls our endpoint. If the vendor offers a public client key with domain restrictions, that key can be a `VITE_` variable because it is already considered public, and the vendor still enforces the restriction.

I would also mention that rotating the secret means rebuilding the SPA if it was inlined.
blocks.explanation: The prefix is an exposure mechanism, not a secrecy mechanism.

blocks.title: The env change that did not ship
blocks.question: Ops updates `VITE_API_BASE_URL` on the host and restarts the static file server. The built SPA still calls the old host. Why?
blocks.answer: Vite replaced `import.meta.env.VITE_API_BASE_URL` with a string when the bundle was built. The static server is not running the Vue app through Vite. The new value is picked up on the next build. Runtime configuration has to be a file or an endpoint the SPA fetches, not a `VITE_` variable, if it must change without a rebuild.
blocks.explanation:
Build-time inlining and runtime environment variables are different tools.

[Further reading](https://vite.dev/guide/env-and-mode.html)
hints: When does Vite read `VITE_` variables for a production bundle?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: The initial JS payload grew by 300 KB after a "small" shared utils folder was added. How do you find the cause?
blocks.answer:
Build with the visualizer and see which new modules landed in the entry chunk. Check whether a route or a component barrel re-exports feature pages, whether a util file imports a heavy library at the top, and whether an icon map imported every view. Move the heavy import behind a dynamic import used by the feature that needs it.

Compare entry size before and after. Do not trust the dev server's network panel as the production graph.
blocks.explanation: A shared folder is a common way to create a static edge from the entry to every feature.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Importing a feature store from `main.ts` "so it is ready".
blocks.whyItHappens: The store module pulls its feature views with it through a barrel, and the lazy route no longer has anything left to load.
blocks.correctApproach: Let the feature's setup call the store. Keep `main.ts` limited to the app shell, router, and Pinia plugin.

blocks.title: Production guidance
blocks.content: Inspect production chunks and treat client env as public.
keyPoints: Verify splits with a production build.
Avoid barrels that re-export routes.
Keep secrets out of `VITE_` variables.
Use a fetched config if a value must change without a rebuild.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
