blocks.content:
Quick revision

- Production chunks follow static and dynamic imports, not the dev server.
- `VITE_` values are inlined and public.
- Changing host env does not change an already built SPA.
- The entry file should not import feature views.

Official references

- https://vite.dev/guide/env-and-mode.html

title: SSR and hydration
description: Why server HTML and the client vnode must match, and where window access belongs.

blocks.title: Hydration reuses the server HTML
blocks.content:
Server rendering runs the Vue app to an HTML string. The browser shows that HTML immediately, then Vue hydrates it: it attaches event listeners and virtual DOM to the existing nodes instead of recreating them. Hydration expects the client's first render to match the server HTML. A mismatch means Vue cannot trust the DOM and will recover by patching or, depending on the case, warn and replace nodes. The user sees a flicker and you lose the benefit of SSR.

Typical mismatches: rendering `Date.now()` or `Math.random()` into the markup, reading `localStorage` or `window` during the first render, invalid HTML nesting that the browser repairs, and a client-only branch that renders different tags than the server.
keyPoints: The first client render must match the server string.
`onMounted` does not run on the server. It is the right place for `window`.
Setup code runs on both sides. A bare `window` read there throws during SSR.
`useId()` exists so ids match across the two renders.

blocks.title: Data for the HTML has to be fetched before the response
blocks.content:
A component that fetches only in `onMounted` renders empty HTML and then fills in on the client. That is a valid SPA strategy. It is not SSR. `onServerPrefetch` or the router's data loader on the server must finish before `renderToString`. The client needs the same data during hydration, usually serialized into the page, or it will render a different tree.

Nuxt is the common production framework around this lifecycle. The Vue core APIs are still the ones to understand in an interview: `renderToString`, hydration, and not touching the DOM during setup. Do not invent Nuxt-only APIs if the app is a plain Vite SSR setup.
keyPoints: Server HTML only includes work that finished before the render.
Send the same payload the server used so the client hydrates against it.
Create a new app and a new Pinia per request. A shared store leaks user A into user B.
Client-only widgets belong behind `onMounted` or a client-only wrapper that renders the same placeholder on the server.

blocks.title: Keep the first render deterministic
blocks.explanation: The greeting depends only on props, so server and client match. The viewport line renders on neither side until mount, so it does not disagree during hydration. `useId` keeps the id stable.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: What is a hydration mismatch, and how do you debug one?
blocks.answer:
The server HTML and the client's first vnode do not describe the same tree. I look at the warning for the node path, then I search that component for `window`, `localStorage`, the current time, random ids, and browser-only branches in the template. I also validate the HTML, because a `

` inside a `

` gets rewritten by the browser before Vue hydrates. The fix is to make the first render a pure function of the props and the serialized payload. Browser-only details start as empty state and update in `onMounted`.
blocks.explanation: Mismatch is a determinism bug. The warning is the start of the search, not the root cause.

blocks.title: The branch that only exists on the client
blocks.question: The template contains `v-if="typeof window !== 'undefined'"`. The server omits the block. Why does hydration still warn?
blocks.answer: On the client, `window` exists during the first render, so the client vnode includes the block and the server HTML does not. The check is not the same on both sides. Start with `const ready = ref(false)`, leave the block hidden, and set `ready.value = true` in `onMounted`. Both sides render the hidden state first.
blocks.explanation:
A browser global is a different value on the server and the client. The first render cannot depend on that difference.

[Further reading](https://vuejs.org/guide/scaling-up/ssr.html)
hints: What is `typeof window` during the client's first render?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: A product page must be indexable, the price must be in the HTML, and a 3D viewer can load later. Users report a flash where the price changes after load. How do you split the work?
blocks.answer:
Fetch the product on the server and render the price from that payload. Serialize the same payload for hydration so the client does not refetch and render a second price before the request returns. Load the 3D viewer as an async component after mount, with a placeholder that was also in the server HTML.

If the price can change every second, SSR is the wrong tool for that number. Render a cached price and update it after hydration with a timestamp that was not baked into two different values.
blocks.explanation: Indexable content is rendered from shared data. Client-only toys start equivalent on both sides, then enhance.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Sharing one Pinia instance and one Vue app across SSR requests.
blocks.whyItHappens: The server process stays warm. State from the previous request is still in the store when the next HTML is rendered.
blocks.correctApproach: Create the app, the router, and Pinia inside the request handler. Dispose of them when the render finishes.

blocks.title: Production guidance
blocks.content: Make the first render a pure function of the request.
keyPoints: No `window` or random values in setup or in the template.
Fetch SSR data before `renderToString` and reuse it on the client.
Use `useId` for generated ids.
Isolate the app instance per request.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- Hydration requires the first client render to match the server HTML.
- `onMounted` is client-only. Setup runs on both sides.
- `typeof window` checks in the template cause mismatches.
- Create a new store and app per server request.

Official references

- https://vuejs.org/guide/scaling-up/ssr.html
- https://vuejs.org/api/composition-api-helpers.html#useid

title: XSS and template safety
description: What Vue escapes, where v-html and URLs bypass that protection, and what the server must still do.

blocks.title: Interpolation is escaped. v-html is not.
blocks.content: Text inside `{{ }}` and text bindings are escaped. A user named `` shows up as text. `v-html` interprets the string as HTML and will run markup you pass in. Use it only for HTML you sanitized or generated yourself. Markdown rendered to HTML counts as HTML: sanitize the output, not just the markdown source, because raw HTML in markdown is a common bypass. Attribute bindings are not a free pass. `:href="userUrl"` can be `javascript:...` on an ``. Allow only `http`, `https`, and relative URLs, or generate the URL on the server. Style bindings should not take a raw user CSS string if that string can inject expressions or URLs.
keyPoints: `{{ }}` escapes. `v-html` does not.
Sanitize before `v-html`, with a maintained library and an explicit tag allowlist.
Validate URL protocols before binding `href` or `src`.
The template compiler is not a security product. The server must encode and authorize too.

blocks.title: Client checks are not the security boundary
blocks.content:
A route guard, a hidden button, and a disabled input are interface choices. The API that mutates data has to authenticate and authorize. XSS matters because it can act as the user: call that API with the user's cookies or token. A strict Content-Security-Policy reduces the damage of injected scripts. Vue's runtime-only build avoids shipping the template compiler, so an attacker who injects a template string still needs a sink such as `v-html` or `eval` to run it.

Do not concatenate user strings into selectors or `innerHTML` inside an `onMounted` "small escape hatch". That bypasses the escaping the template would have done.
keyPoints: Prefer the runtime-only build so templates are compiled at build time.
CSP is a backstop, not a replacement for escaping.
Cookies used by the API should be `HttpOnly` and `SameSite` where the architecture allows it.
Rendering another user's content is the threat model. Your own static markdown in the repo is a different risk.

blocks.title: Allow only http(s) links from user content
blocks.explanation: The template binds `:href="safeHttpUrl(userUrl) ?? undefined"` and does not render the anchor when the helper returns null. `javascript:` and protocol-relative URLs fail the check.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: Is Vue safe from XSS by default?
blocks.answer:
Vue escapes text interpolations, which removes the most common sink. It is not a blanket guarantee. `v-html`, unsanitized markdown, `javascript:` URLs, dynamic `<component :is="userString">` against a full component map, and manual DOM writes are all sinks. I would also say the API must assume the client is hostile, because XSS is not the only way to call it.

A good answer names the sink and the server control, not "Vue sanitizes everything".
blocks.explanation: Default escaping covers `{{ }}`. Every other HTML sink is opt-in and dangerous.

blocks.title: The markdown preview
blocks.question: A preview pane runs a markdown library and binds the result with `v-html`. The library leaves raw HTML in the output. A user pastes ``. What runs, and what do you change?
blocks.answer: The browser parses that string as HTML because `v-html` does not escape, and the `onerror` handler runs if the image errors. Sanitize the HTML with an allowlist after markdown conversion, or configure the markdown parser to disallow raw HTML and still sanitize. Do not sanitize only the original markdown source and then trust the HTML converter.
blocks.explanation:
Markdown-to-HTML is an HTML sink. The escape hatch is the binding, not the editor widget.

[Further reading](https://vuejs.org/guide/best-practices/security.html)
hints: Does `v-html` escape its value?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: Support agents need to see customers' submitted HTML descriptions. How do you render them in the admin Vue app?
blocks.answer:
Sanitize on the server with a strict allowlist and render that sanitized string with `v-html`, or render a safe subset as Vue text and links you generate yourself. I would rather not store "HTML" at all. A structured document (paragraphs, links with validated URLs) is easier to render with templates.

The admin app is still a victim if it renders attacker HTML. Internal users are not a reason to skip sanitizing. CSP should disallow inline event handlers.
blocks.explanation: The trust boundary is the content's author, not the role of the person viewing it.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Binding `:href="userUrl"` and assuming Vue escapes it like `{{ userUrl }}`.
blocks.whyItHappens: Escaping text content does not restrict URL protocols. The attribute is still a URL the browser will navigate.
blocks.correctApproach: Allowlist protocols or emit only URLs you created.

blocks.title: Production guidance
blocks.content: Keep HTML out of user strings unless a sanitizer stands in front of `v-html`.
keyPoints: Default to interpolation.
Sanitize markdown HTML output.
Validate URLs before binding.
Authorize on the server even when the button is hidden.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- `{{ }}` escapes text. `v-html` interprets HTML.
- URL bindings need a protocol allowlist.
- Client UI checks are not authorization.
- Prefer the runtime-only build and a CSP as defense in depth.

Official references

- https://vuejs.org/guide/best-practices/security.html

title: Auth tokens and session boundaries
description: Where a Vue SPA should keep a session, and what logout must erase.

blocks.title: The browser is a hostile place to store a secret
blocks.content:
A Vue SPA cannot hide a token from its own JavaScript. Anything in `localStorage`, session storage, or a Pinia store is readable by any script running on the origin, including an XSS payload. An `HttpOnly` cookie cannot be read by JavaScript, which is why many apps ask the server to set the session cookie and let the browser send it. That choice requires CSRF protection for cookie-authenticated requests: a same-site cookie policy, a CSRF token, or both, depending on the API.

If the architecture uses a bearer token in memory, a refresh leaves the user signed out unless there is a refresh cookie. That trade-off is acceptable for some apps. Writing the bearer token into `localStorage` for convenience is the part to challenge in an interview.
keyPoints: Vue code cannot keep a secret from other scripts on the page.
`HttpOnly` cookies are not readable from the SPA. Memory tokens are readable and disappear on refresh.
Route guards only choose screens. The API rejects missing or insufficient sessions.
Logout clears memory, resets stores, and asks the server to revoke the session.

blocks.title: Account switches must drop the previous user's data
blocks.content:
Pinia, a query cache, `localStorage` drafts, and a module-level ref all survive a component unmount. `signOut` has to clear them or the next person on a shared computer sees the previous inbox. A second tab needs a policy too: `storage` events or a `BroadcastChannel` can tell other tabs to reset. Without that, tab A logs out and tab B still shows the old store until the next request fails.

Do not log tokens, and do not put them in route params or error reports.
keyPoints: List every cache that holds user data and clear it on logout.
Tell other tabs that the session ended.
Failed refresh should go to a signed-out state once, not retry in a loop.
Authorization checks use server data (role, tenant), not a boolean the client set.

blocks.title: Reset user-scoped stores on sign-out
blocks.explanation: The server revokes the cookie session first. Then the client drops in-memory stores and session storage. A real app would reset every user-scoped store, not only the cart, and would broadcast the logout to other tabs.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: Where would you store an access token in a Vue SPA, and what would you refuse?
blocks.answer:
I prefer an `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite` session cookie set by the server, with CSRF defenses on state-changing requests, because XSS cannot read the cookie. If we must use a bearer token, I keep it in memory and accept the refresh-to-login behavior, or pair it with a refresh cookie. I refuse `localStorage` for long-lived access tokens because every XSS becomes an account takeover that survives a reload.

I would also say the Vue route guard is not the control. The API is.
blocks.explanation: The storage choice is about XSS blast radius, not about which Vue API is convenient.

blocks.title: The guard that trusted the store
blocks.question: A `beforeEach` guard allows `/admin` when `userStore.role === "admin"`. The role was set from a decoded JWT payload on the client. The API also checks the token signature and role. Is the admin UI safe?
blocks.answer: The UI is not a security boundary. Anyone can flip the store and see the admin screens' layout, which may leak how the product works, but they should not receive admin data if the API checks the signature and role. If an admin request succeeds after the flip, the API bug is the real finding. Also, decoding a JWT without verifying it is not a role lookup. The client display role should come from a server response, and it still is not authorization.
blocks.explanation:
Client role flags are for showing and hiding navigation. The server decides access.

[Further reading](https://router.vuejs.org/guide/advanced/navigation-guards.html)
hints: Which system is allowed to decide that a request succeeds?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: Two agents share a kiosk browser. Agent A logs out, and agent B sees A's cached customer list for a second before the route changes. What do you clear, and when?
blocks.answer:
Clear user-scoped stores and in-memory caches before navigating to the login screen, not after the next user's dashboard fetches. Abort in-flight requests so a late response cannot refill the cache. Wipe `sessionStorage` drafts. If customer data was written to `localStorage` or IndexedDB, delete those keys too.

On a kiosk, prefer a short session and a server-side revoke so a copied cookie from earlier does not work.
blocks.explanation: Logout is a data-lifetime event. Navigation alone does not clear a store.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Saving the access token in Pinia and persisting Pinia to `localStorage` with a plugin "so refresh works".
blocks.whyItHappens: The plugin is generic, so every ref, including the token and the customer cache, is persisted.
blocks.correctApproach: Persist only non-sensitive preferences. Keep the session in an `HttpOnly` cookie or an in-memory token with a refresh flow you designed.

blocks.title: Production guidance
blocks.content: Design logout as carefully as login.
keyPoints: Prefer `HttpOnly` cookies over readable token storage.
Authorize on the API.
Reset every user cache and abort requests on logout.
Notify other tabs.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- SPA JavaScript cannot hide secrets from XSS.
- `HttpOnly` cookies move the secret out of Vue's reach and require CSRF protection.
- Guards pick screens. APIs authorize.
- Logout revokes the server session and clears client caches.

Official references

- https://vuejs.org/guide/best-practices/security.html
- https://router.vuejs.org/guide/advanced/navigation-guards.html

title: KeepAlive and Teleport
description: Cached instances versus destroyed ones, and how teleported DOM relates to the component tree.

blocks.title: KeepAlive caches the instance instead of destroying it
blocks.content:
`<KeepAlive>` stores a child component's instance when it is switched out, so the next visit restores state. `onUnmounted` does not run when the view is hidden. `onDeactivated` does. `onActivated` runs when it is shown again, including the first time after mount. Use these hooks to pause a video, a poll, or a chart animation.

`include` and `exclude` match the component's `name`. A `<script setup>` component needs `defineOptions({ name: "ReportTab" })` or the include list will not see it. `max` drops the least recently used instance. A cache without a max, holding pages that each hold a large list, is a memory leak with a framework API.
keyPoints: Deactivated is not unmounted. Clean up resources that should pause.
Include/exclude use the component name.
Set `max` when the cached trees are heavy.
A cached page that watches a route param still needs that watch. Activation is not a new param hook.

blocks.title: Teleport moves DOM, not component ownership
blocks.content:
`<Teleport to="body">` renders its slot content at another DOM node, usually so a modal escapes `overflow: hidden` or a stacking context. The teleported nodes still belong to the parent component for props, emits, provide/inject, and Vue lifecycle. Native DOM events bubble through the real DOM parents, which are outside the Vue parent. A click listener on a Vue ancestor will not see a native click from inside the teleport via Vue's component tree.

Vue 3.5 added deferred teleport so the target can exist after the initial render. Teleporting to a missing target warns. On SSR, the target must make sense in the server HTML or you should defer until the client.
keyPoints: Provide/inject still follows the Vue parent, not the DOM parent.
Native events follow the DOM tree.
A modal should restore focus to the opener when it closes.
Do not teleport a form out of its `<form>` and expect the browser submit to include those fields. The DOM moved.

blocks.title: Pause a poll while a kept-alive tab is hidden
blocks.code:
<script setup lang="ts">
import { onActivated, onDeactivated, ref } from 'vue'

defineOptions({ name: 'PricesTab' })
const price = ref(0)
let timer: ReturnType<typeof setInterval> | undefined

function start() {
  stop()
  timer = setInterval(() => { price.value += 1 }, 1000)
}
function stop() {
  if (timer) clearInterval(timer)
  timer = undefined
}

onActivated(start)
onDeactivated(stop)
</script>
blocks.explanation: The parent wraps this tab in `<KeepAlive include="PricesTab">`. Leaving the tab deactivates it and stops the interval. Coming back starts a new one. `onUnmounted` would not run on a tab switch.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: Why does a modal often use Teleport, and what bugs does that create?
blocks.answer:
Teleport avoids ancestor CSS such as `overflow`, `transform`, and `z-index` trapping the overlay. The bugs are focus and events. Focus can move into a node that is logically "in" the component but physically at the end of `body`, so you must trap focus and restore it. A click-outside detector that listens on the Vue root may not see the teleported panel the way the author expected, because native bubbling follows `body`.

I also check SSR. A target that exists only in the client needs a deferred teleport or a client-only mount.
blocks.explanation: Teleport is a DOM placement tool. Component ownership stays put, and native bubbling does not.

blocks.title: The timer that survives a tab switch
blocks.question: A tab is inside `<KeepAlive>` and starts a `setInterval` in `onMounted` with `clearInterval` in `onUnmounted`. Users switch tabs and the network panel keeps polling. Why?
blocks.answer: Switching away deactivates the cached component. It does not unmount it, so `onUnmounted` does not run and the interval continues. Clear the interval in `onDeactivated`, and start it in `onActivated`. Also clear in `onUnmounted` for when the cache finally drops the instance.
blocks.explanation:
Cached views have a second pair of hooks. Unmount is only the final one.

[Further reading](https://vuejs.org/guide/built-ins/keep-alive.html)
hints: Which hook runs when KeepAlive hides a child?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: A multi-step wizard is kept alive so people can go back without losing fields. Step three opens a confirmation modal teleported to `body`. Screen-reader focus escapes the dialog, and submitting the wizard misses the confirmation checkbox. What do you fix?
blocks.answer:
Trap focus inside the dialog and return focus to the button that opened it. Give the dialog `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal`. Do not rely on the visual overlay alone.

Then check the checkbox DOM. If it was teleported outside the `<form>`, it is not a form participant. Keep the input in the form and teleport only the visual shell, or read the checkbox from the draft state instead of from `FormData`. `KeepAlive` is unrelated to the missing field, but it does mean the wizard's draft survives the modal closing, which is what you want.
blocks.explanation: KeepAlive preserves the wizard instance. Teleport can pull controls out of the form DOM. Handle both on purpose.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Matching `<KeepAlive include="Report">` while the SFC never sets a name.
blocks.whyItHappens: The file name feels like the component name. Script setup components are anonymous unless `defineOptions` or the name option sets it.
blocks.correctApproach: Set `defineOptions({ name: "Report" })` and test that leaving the route restores state only for the named view.

blocks.title: Production guidance
blocks.content: Use KeepAlive for expensive or draft-heavy views, with a max and pause hooks. Use Teleport for stacking, not for data flow.
keyPoints: Pair `onActivated` and `onDeactivated` with mount and unmount cleanup.
Name components that an include list targets.
Remember teleported content inherits Vue context and DOM position separately.
Restore focus for dialogs.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- `KeepAlive` deactivates instead of unmounting.
- `include` matches component names.
- Teleport changes the DOM parent, not the Vue parent.
- Native events and HTML forms follow the DOM.

Official references

- https://vuejs.org/guide/built-ins/keep-alive.html
- https://vuejs.org/guide/built-ins/teleport.html

title: Component testing
description: What to mount, what to assert, and how Vue Test Utils interacts with reactivity.

blocks.title: Test behavior the user can see
blocks.content:
Mount the component with `@vue/test-utils`, pass props, and interact through the DOM: `await wrapper.get('button').trigger('click')`, then assert the text, the attributes, or the emitted events. That survives a refactor from `ref` to `computed`. Asserting `wrapper.vm.count` ties the test to a private binding that `<script setup>` does not even expose.

Stub child components when the child has its own tests and the parent only needs to pass props. Do not stub the component you are trying to prove. A page test that stubs every child asserts nothing about the page.
keyPoints: Prefer DOM assertions and emitted events over `wrapper.vm`.
Await updates. Test Utils flushes Vue's reactivity when you await a trigger, but a real `fetch` needs a flushed promise you control.
Provide injected dependencies in the mount options.
Create a fresh Pinia per test when the component uses a store.

blocks.title: Async tests need a deterministic clock and network
blocks.content:
Mock `fetch` or inject an API function. Resolve it when the test says so, then `await flushPromises()` or await the wrapper's next update before asserting. A test that hopes the real network returns is slow and flaky.

Timers and `watch` debounces should use Vitest's fake timers. Advance time, then flush promises, because a debounce often schedules a timer that then awaits a request.
keyPoints: Do not call the real network from a unit test.
Assert the loading state and the error state, not only the happy path.
A stale-response test resolves the older request last.
Accessibility checks belong here too: label text, `aria-invalid`, and button names.

blocks.title: Assert an emit instead of private state
blocks.explanation: The test uses the label-free input only because this example has one control. A real form should `get` by label. The contract under test is the `save` event, which the parent will handle.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: What do you avoid asserting in a Vue component test?
blocks.answer:
I avoid private refs, the exact number of renders, and snapshots of the entire HTML that fail when a class name changes. I assert the behavior: given these props, after this input, the user sees this error or the component emits this payload. I also avoid mounting the whole router and every provider if a smaller mount with stubs can prove the same contract.

I do mount enough of the real component to catch template mistakes. A test of a function that returns vnodes without the real template can miss a broken `v-if`.
blocks.explanation: The test should fail when the user-visible contract breaks, not when the implementation moves.

blocks.title: The assertion that ran too early
blocks.question: A test calls `wrapper.get('button').trigger('click')` without `await`, then immediately expects the loading text. The component sets `loading.value = true` inside the click handler before an `await fetch`. Why does the assertion flake?
blocks.answer: The DOM updates after Vue flushes the reactive write, and `trigger` returns a promise that includes that flush. Without awaiting it, the assertion reads the old DOM. Await the trigger. If the text depends on the fetch resolving, flush that promise too before asserting the result.
blocks.explanation:
The state changed in the handler. The DOM the test reads updates on the flush that `await trigger` waits for.

[Further reading](https://vuejs.org/guide/scaling-up/testing.html)
hints: When does Vue write the new text into the DOM?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: A page test mounts the real router, Pinia, three feature stores, and the design system, and it fails whenever an unrelated store's initial state changes. How do you narrow it?
blocks.answer:
Test the page's own contract with injected fakes: a `loadCustomer` function, a router mock that only supplies the param, and stubbed children that emit. Move store logic to store unit tests. Keep one thicker test for the wiring, not twenty.

If the failure is "missing provide", that is a useful signal that the component has a hidden dependency. Provide it explicitly in `global.provide` so the dependency stays visible.
blocks.explanation: Broad mounts hide the contract. Inject the boundary the component actually needs.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Calling `wrapper.vm.submit()` on a `<script setup>` component.
blocks.whyItHappens: The method exists in the module but is not on the instance proxy unless it was exposed. The test then pushes the author to `defineExpose` a method that only tests needed.
blocks.correctApproach: Submit the form through the DOM. Expose methods only when production parents call them.

blocks.title: Production guidance
blocks.content: Mount the component, drive the DOM, assert the contract.
keyPoints: Await triggers and flushed requests.
Stub children that have their own tests.
Give each test a fresh Pinia.
Cover error, empty, and stale-response paths.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- Assert DOM and events, not private setup bindings.
- Await `trigger` so the render flush has happened.
- Mock the network and inject providers.
- Do not `defineExpose` just for tests.

Official references

- https://vuejs.org/guide/scaling-up/testing.html

title: Testing composables
description: How to run a composable with an active effect scope and prove cleanup.

blocks.title: A composable needs an active instance or a scope
blocks.content:
Calling `useSearch()` in a bare Vitest test can warn that there is no active instance, and its `onUnmounted` hook will never run. Two honest setups exist. Mount a tiny host component whose setup calls the composable and returns the bindings for the test. Or run the composable inside `effectScope()`, stop the scope, and assert that timers and watchers ended.

The host component is better when the composable uses lifecycle hooks. `effectScope` is better when you want to prove that `scope.stop()` drops a watch without mounting a template.
keyPoints: Do not call lifecycle-aware composables in a naked test.
`effectScope().run(() => useX())` gives the effects an owner.
`scope.stop()` is the unmount equivalent for those effects.
Pass refs in so the test can change inputs without a DOM.

blocks.title: Prove the cleanup, not only the first value
blocks.content:
A composable that registers `addEventListener` or `setInterval` should be tested by stopping the scope or unmounting the host and then firing the event or advancing the timer. If the callback still changes state, the cleanup is missing.

Async composables need the same stale-response test as components. Start two ids, resolve the first after the second, and expect the first payload to be ignored.
keyPoints: A test that only checks the initial ref misses leaks.
Use fake timers for intervals.
AbortController tests should abort and then resolve the old fetch.
Do not share a module-level ref across tests. Reset it or create state inside the composable.

blocks.title: Run a composable in an effect scope
blocks.explanation: `scope.run` is the owner that `watch` and `computed` inside `useDouble` attach to. `scope.stop()` disposes them so later tests do not keep those effects.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: When would you mount a component instead of using `effectScope` to test a composable?
blocks.answer:
When the composable calls `onMounted`, `onUnmounted`, or reads template refs and injected values. A one-line host component exercises those hooks with `mount` and `unmount`. `effectScope` does not simulate a DOM mount.

I still unit-test a pure derivation with a scope or even a direct call if it uses only `computed` and no lifecycle. The heavier mount is for integration with Vue's instance, not for every function.
blocks.explanation: Pick the smallest owner that actually implements the hooks the composable uses.

blocks.title: The watcher that survives the test
blocks.question: A test calls `useQuery(query)` with no `effectScope` and no mount. `useQuery` registers a `watch` on the query. Later tests change unrelated refs and still see fetch mocks from this watch. Why?
blocks.answer: The watch was created on a detached scope that nobody stopped, or on a leaked component instance. It stays active for the rest of the Vitest process. Run it inside an effect scope and `stop()` in a `finally`, or mount a host and `unmount()` it. Also check that `useQuery` does not store the watch in a module-level singleton.
blocks.explanation:
Effects do not disappear because the test function returned. They disappear when their scope stops.

[Further reading](https://vuejs.org/guide/reusability/composables.html)
hints: Who is responsible for stopping a watch created in a composable?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: A composable works in the app and fails in CI with "onMounted is called when there is no active component instance". Developers wrap the call in `try/catch` inside the composable. What do you do instead?
blocks.answer:
Remove the try/catch. The warning is telling you the test called a lifecycle composable outside setup. Mount a host or document that `useX` must run in setup. Swallowing the warning means the listener is never registered in the test, so the test passes while the cleanup path is untested.

If a composable must work both inside and outside components, give it an explicit `effectScope` argument rather than detecting the instance with a blank catch.
blocks.explanation: The error is the test harness, not a production branch to hide.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Asserting a composable's behavior by mounting the entire page that happens to use it.
blocks.whyItHappens: The page test is already there. It is slow, and a failure does not say which input the composable mishandled.
blocks.correctApproach: Give the composable a direct test with refs as inputs. Leave the page test for wiring.

blocks.title: Production guidance
blocks.content: Give every composable test an owner and a stop.
keyPoints: Use `effectScope` for watch and computed logic.
Mount a host when lifecycle hooks matter.
Assert that stop or unmount cancels timers and listeners.
Resolve stale requests out of order.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- Composables that register effects need an instance or an effect scope.
- `scope.stop()` is the test's unmount.
- Prove cleanup, not only the initial value.
- Do not swallow the "no active instance" warning.

Official references

- https://vuejs.org/guide/reusability/composables.html
- https://vuejs.org/guide/scaling-up/testing.html

title: Contract testing with backend teams
description: How a Vue client and an API stay compatible without sharing a database in unit tests.

blocks.title: The contract is the payload, not a screenshot of the UI
blocks.content:
Frontend and backend teams break each other when a field becomes nullable or changes meaning. A contract test pins the request and response shape. Consumer-driven contracts (for example Pact) let the Vue client publish the interactions it depends on, and the API build verifies them. An OpenAPI schema plus generated types helps the client compile against the documented shape, but a schema that the server does not actually check is documentation, not a contract.

Validate at the edge in the client too. TypeScript types disappear at runtime. A parser such as Zod for the responses you render will fail in a test or a monitoring event instead of throwing halfway down a template.
keyPoints: Generated types are not runtime checks.
Contract tests should run in CI on both sides.
Nullable and missing are different. Pin both.
A fixture checked into the Vue repo rots unless the API build uses the same example.

blocks.title: Failures should name the field and the version
blocks.content:
When a contract fails, the error should say which interaction and which field, not "snapshot mismatch" of an entire page. Version the API. The Vue app should send the version it understands and render a recoverable error when the server reports an unsupported one.

Do not point unit tests at a shared staging API. They will flake and they will hide contract gaps until staging is down. Run contract tests against the provider's verification step, and run UI tests against mocks that were produced from the contract.
keyPoints: Mocks in component tests should match the contract examples.
Staging smoke tests are extra. They do not replace a contract.
Breaking changes need a version or a compatibility window.
Auth headers and error envelopes are part of the contract, not an afterthought.

blocks.title: Parse the payload before it reaches a component
blocks.explanation: The component receives a `Customer`, not `unknown`. A contract fixture that drops `seats` fails in `parseCustomer` during the client test and, if the same schema is shared or the interaction is verified, on the API side too.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: The backend renamed `fullName` to `name` and the Vue page renders blanks with no error. What process do you add?
blocks.answer:
I add a contract interaction for the customer response that expects `name`, and I parse the response before render so a missing field throws in CI instead of interpolating empty text. The API verification runs those interactions. For the rollout, I would accept both fields for one version or ship the client and server together behind a versioned endpoint.

I would not "fix" it by optional-chaining every field in the template. That turns a broken contract into a silent blank UI.
blocks.explanation: Silence is the failure mode of unchecked JSON. Parsing and a verified contract make the break loud.

blocks.title: The type that lied
blocks.question: The client has `http.get<Customer>()`, or a hand-written `as Customer`. The server removed `seats`. TypeScript still compiles. What protection did the generic or the cast actually give you?
blocks.answer: None at runtime. The generic and the cast tell the compiler what you hope the JSON is. They do not check the payload. A parser or a contract test is what fails when `seats` disappears.
blocks.explanation:
Compile-time types and runtime JSON are different layers. The interview expects you to say so.

[Further reading](https://vuejs.org/guide/scaling-up/testing.html)
hints: Does the TypeScript type exist after compilation?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: Teams deploy the SPA and the API independently, often hours apart. How do you keep a breaking field change from becoming a Friday incident?
blocks.answer:
The API adds the new field while still sending the old one. The contract allows both for a window. The SPA starts reading the new field, ships, and then the API removes the old field in a later deploy after the contract drops it. CI fails either side if it jumps the gun.

Feature flags can hide a UI that depends on the new field, but they do not replace the compatibility window if the old client is still cached in users' browsers.
blocks.explanation: Independent deploys require a compatibility window. A cached SPA is an old client you did not mean to keep.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Updating a hand-copied JSON fixture in the Vue repo and forgetting the API tests still emit the old shape.
blocks.whyItHappens: The frontend test goes green because it mocked itself. Production still sends the old payload.
blocks.correctApproach: Generate or verify fixtures from the contract the API build runs.

blocks.title: Production guidance
blocks.content: Make response shape a CI failure on both repositories.
keyPoints: Parse untrusted JSON at the edge.
Verify consumer interactions against the provider.
Version or overlap fields when deploys are independent.
Remember browsers will keep an old SPA bundle.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- Types and casts do not validate JSON.
- Contract tests pin the interactions both teams share.
- Parse before render so a missing field is loud.
- Independent deploys need an overlap window.

Official references

- https://vuejs.org/guide/scaling-up/testing.html

title: Component API design
description: How to keep a shared Vue component small enough to reuse.

blocks.title: A component API is props, emits, and slots
blocks.content:
Those three are the contract. Props configure. Emits report. Slots let the parent own layout that the component cannot predict. When a shared button grows `variant`, `size`, `iconLeft`, `iconRight`, `loading`, `href`, and `block`, the next request should be a new component or a slot, not an eleventh prop.

Document the defaults and the controlled-versus-uncontrolled choice. A menu that sometimes owns `open` and sometimes uses `v-model:open` will get both out of sync. Pick controlled if the parent must coordinate, and uncontrolled if it does not.
keyPoints: Prefer a small prop set of primitives and unions.
Use slots when the parent supplies structure.
Do not expose internal refs as the API if an emit can carry the fact.
Name boolean props for the state (`disabled`, `open`), not for the action (`disable`).

blocks.title: Wrappers stay thin
blocks.content:
A design-system field wraps a native input. It forwards attrs, associates a label, and emits the model. It does not fetch options, talk to Pinia, or know which page it is on. Feature components compose fields and call stores. When a field knows about the customer store, you cannot reuse it on the vendor screen.

Version a breaking prop rename. A shared package that deletes `value` in favor of `modelValue` overnight breaks every app that had not upgraded the template.
keyPoints: Presentational components do not import feature stores.
Feature containers own data loading.
Forward attrs to the native control.
Breaking a public prop is a release event.

blocks.title: A small disclosure API
blocks.explanation: The parent can leave `open` uncontrolled or bind `v-model:open`. Content is a slot, so the disclosure does not grow a prop per use case. `aria-expanded` is part of the contract, not an optional extra.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: How do you push back on a component that has collected 40 props?
blocks.answer:
I group the props by who changes them. Visual variants that are really layout become slots. Data that only one screen needs moves back to that screen. A rare combination becomes a separate component instead of `mode="special"`. I keep a prop when many callers pass the same primitive and the component can render it accessibly.

Then I look at emits. If parents are watching internal state through extra props because the component does not emit the right event, I add the event and delete the workaround props.
blocks.explanation: The split is about who owns the variation, not about an arbitrary prop count.

blocks.title: The boolean that meant three things
blocks.question: A table has `loading`, and callers pass `true` for the initial fetch, for a refresh, and for a row action. The table hides all rows whenever `loading` is true, so a row save blanks the page. What is wrong with the API?
blocks.answer: One boolean is doing three jobs. The table should separate `status` of the whole collection from `pendingRowId` or an emitting row action. Hiding rows is a decision about the initial empty load, not about every boolean named loading.
blocks.explanation:
A vague prop forces every caller into the same UI. Name the states.

[Further reading](https://vuejs.org/guide/components/props.html)
hints: Which user-visible states were collapsed into one prop?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: Two teams share a `UserPicker`. One needs async search. The other has 20 static options. Both are pushing props into the same component (`fetchUrl`, `staticItems`, `debounce`, `headers`). How do you split it?
blocks.answer:
The picker component receives `options`, `query`, and emits `update:query` and `update:modelValue`. It does not fetch. The async team wraps it with a composable that debounces and loads. The static team passes an array. Shared visual behavior stays in one place without a prop matrix.

If the fetch URL had stayed inside the picker, every new auth header would have changed a design-system component.
blocks.explanation: Data loading and picking are different APIs. Compose them.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Emitting the whole internal draft on every private helper call so parents can "stay in sync".
blocks.whyItHappens: It avoids a controlled model and leaks partial states the parent then starts depending on.
blocks.correctApproach: Emit deliberate events: `submit`, `cancel`, and a controlled `update:modelValue` if the parent owns the value.

blocks.title: Production guidance
blocks.content: Design the component as if a second app will consume it.
keyPoints: Props, emits, and slots are the whole public surface.
Keep IO and feature stores out of presentational components.
Split a prop that means more than one state.
Treat renames as breaking changes.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- Small prop sets, explicit emits, slots for open-ended content.
- Do not overload one boolean with several states.
- Presentational components do not fetch.
- Controlled or uncontrolled, not both by accident.

Official references

- https://vuejs.org/guide/components/props.html
- https://vuejs.org/guide/components/slots.html

title: Accessibility in Vue components
description: Labels, focus, keyboard behavior, and the extra care teleported dialogs need.

blocks.title: Use the native control before inventing one
blocks.content:
A `<button>` is focusable, activates with Enter and Space, and has a button role. A `<div @click>` has none of that until you add it back, and teams forget the keyboard half. Prefer native inputs, buttons, and links. When you build a listbox or a dialog, follow the ARIA pattern: roles, keyboard handling, and focus movement.

Labels are not placeholders. A placeholder disappears. Associate `<label for>` with the input id. `useId()` gives you an id that survives SSR. Errors connect with `aria-describedby` and `aria-invalid`.
keyPoints: Native elements bring keyboard behavior you would otherwise reimplement.
Every control has an accessible name.
Do not remove focus outlines without a replacement.
Color is not the only signal for errors or status.

blocks.title: Focus is part of the component lifecycle
blocks.content:
Opening a dialog moves focus into it. Closing it returns focus to the element that opened it. Vue will not do this because a `v-if` appeared. You write it, often in a watcher after `nextTick`, because the input does not exist until the DOM updates. Teleport does not change that duty. It makes the DOM location different from the component parent, so a focus trap has to look at the teleported nodes.

Route changes should move focus to the new page heading, or screen-reader users stay at the bottom of the previous page. The router does not announce navigation by itself.
keyPoints: Store the opener element before you move focus.
Restore focus even when the dialog closes because of Escape or a route change.
A focus trap must allow Tab to wrap inside the dialog and must release on close.
Live regions (`aria-live`) announce async results. Do not rely on a spinner alone.

blocks.title: Name a control and describe its error
blocks.explanation: The label's `for` matches the input. The error is a separate element referenced by `aria-describedby` only while it exists. Ids come from `useId()` so two fields, and a server render, do not collide.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: What do you review on a custom dropdown before it ships?
blocks.answer:
I check that it has a button with `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls`, that arrow keys move the active option, that Enter selects, that Escape closes and restores focus, and that the listbox is labeled. I check the typeahead and disabled options. I then try it with only the keyboard and with a screen reader, because a mouse-only demo hides the gaps.

If the team cannot own that behavior, I prefer a native `<select>` or a maintained library rather than a styled div list.
blocks.explanation: A custom widget inherits a spec. "It looks like a dropdown" is not the spec.

blocks.title: The clickable div
blocks.question: A card uses `<div @click="open">` and a CSS hover state. Mouse users can open it. Keyboard users cannot tab to it. What is missing, and what should you use instead?
blocks.answer: The div is not in the tab order and has no button role or key handler. Use a `<button type="button">` if it performs an action, or an `<a href>` if it navigates. Adding `tabindex="0"` and a keydown handler is the fallback when the design truly cannot use a native control, and it must include Enter and Space plus a visible focus style.
blocks.explanation:
Click handlers do not add keyboard access. The element type is the accessibility API.

[Further reading](https://vuejs.org/guide/best-practices/accessibility.html)
hints: Which elements are focusable by default?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: A modal inside `v-if`, teleported to `body`, traps focus in testing but not when a validation error appears and moves the buttons. What do you retest?
blocks.answer:
The focus trap's node list was probably captured once when the dialog opened. Rebuild the list when the dialog content changes, or query the focusable elements on each Tab. Confirm focus still returns to the opener if the error state unmounts the original button inside the dialog.

Also retest with the teleported DOM: the trap should query inside the dialog element, not inside the Vue parent's root, because the nodes are under `body`.
blocks.explanation: Focus traps that snapshot nodes go stale when Vue adds or removes controls.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Using `placeholder` as the only label and clearing the error text without updating `aria-invalid`.
blocks.whyItHappens: The screen looks labeled while you are typing. The accessible name is empty, and the invalid state sticks or disappears incorrectly.
blocks.correctApproach: Keep a visible label, toggle `aria-invalid` with the error, and point `aria-describedby` at the message.

blocks.title: Production guidance
blocks.content: Ship keyboard behavior and names with the component, not as a later pass.
keyPoints: Prefer native controls.
Pair labels and errors with stable ids.
Move and restore focus when dialogs open and close.
Announce async status with a live region.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- Native buttons and inputs bring keyboard behavior.
- `useId` pairs labels, controls, and errors.
- Dialogs move focus in and put it back.
- Teleport changes where the nodes are, not the obligation.

Official references

- https://vuejs.org/guide/best-practices/accessibility.html
- https://vuejs.org/api/composition-api-helpers.html#useid

title: Third-party widget integration
description: How to host a chart, map, or editor that mutates the DOM itself.

blocks.title: The library owns its DOM. Vue owns the element around it.
blocks.content:
Charting, map, and rich-text libraries often write directly to a DOM node and keep internal instances. If Vue rerenders that subtree and replaces the node, the library is left holding a detached element. Give the library a dedicated element via a template ref, create the instance in `onMounted`, and destroy it in `onUnmounted`. Mark the instance `markRaw` so Vue does not proxy it.

Do not bind the library's internal HTML with `v-html` on each update. Push data into the instance API (`chart.updateSeries`, `editor.setContent`) from a watcher.
keyPoints: Create on mount, destroy on unmount, pause on deactivate if kept alive.
`markRaw` the instance and `toRaw` any state you hand it if it must mutate freely.
One element, one owner. Do not let Vue and the library both manage the same children.
If the library emits DOM events, bridge them to Vue emits at the boundary.

blocks.title: Updates are imperative and explicit
blocks.content:
A watcher on the data you care about calls the library. `{ flush: 'post' }` is appropriate when the call measures the element. Cleanup inside the watcher cancels a scheduled frame or a pending `setData` if the source changes quickly.

SSR cannot construct these libraries if they touch `window`. The server renders a placeholder with the same dimensions so layout does not jump, and the client constructs the library after mount. Hydration should not expect the library's private DOM to match Vue's vnode children, because Vue should not be rendering those children.
keyPoints: Watch data, call the instance. Do not recreate the instance to change data.
Placeholder on the server, enhance on the client.
Load the library with a dynamic import so pages that do not show it do not pay for it.
Pin the library version. Widget APIs break more quietly than Vue APIs.

blocks.title: Own a chart instance beside Vue
blocks.explanation: Vue renders an empty host. The library fills it after mount. Data changes call `setData` instead of remounting. `destroy` releases canvases and listeners. `deep` is acceptable here only because `points` is a small series, not a huge document.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: How do you stop a map library from leaking after users leave the page?
blocks.answer:
I keep the instance in the component, not in a module singleton, and I call its documented destroy method in `onUnmounted`. If the page is inside `KeepAlive`, I also stop animations in `onDeactivated` and destroy only on unmount. I verify with a heap snapshot after navigating away twice.

If the library registers `window` listeners and its destroy is incomplete, I wrap it and remove those listeners myself, and I file the leak against the version we pinned.
blocks.explanation: The integration owns the lifetime because Vue does not know about the library's subscriptions.

blocks.title: Vue rerendered the library's node
blocks.question:
The chart host is `
{{ caption }}
`. Updating `caption` makes the chart go blank even though the instance still exists. Why?
blocks.answer: Vue patches the host's children when `caption` changes and can wipe the DOM the chart inserted. The host element that Vue manages should be empty. Put the caption in a sibling node. The chart is the only writer of the host's contents.
blocks.explanation:
Two owners of one element's inner DOM will overwrite each other on the next patch.

[Further reading](https://vuejs.org/guide/essentials/template-refs.html)
hints: Who is allowed to change the host element's children?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: A rich-text editor must post sanitized HTML, support SSR pages, and not freeze the tab when the document is large. How do you integrate it?
blocks.answer:
Load the editor on the client only, inside a host element, after mount. Keep the source of truth in your draft ref, but do not push every keystroke back through `v-html`. Listen to the editor's change event and update the draft. Sanitize on submit on the server, and sanitize before any other view renders the HTML.

For a large document, do not deep-reactive the editor's internal model. `markRaw` the editor. If `v-model` from the parent echoes into `setContent` on every local change, guard the watcher so it does not reset the cursor.
blocks.explanation: The editor is imperative. Vue holds the submitted value, not the caret and the internal DOM.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Storing the chart instance in a `reactive` object so "Vue can track it".
blocks.whyItHappens: The proxy breaks private fields or confuses equality, and it does not help because you never render the instance.
blocks.correctApproach: `markRaw` it or keep it in a plain `let`. Track the data, not the widget.

blocks.title: Production guidance
blocks.content: Give the widget a host element, a create/destroy pair, and an update method.
keyPoints: Empty host. Sibling Vue nodes for labels.
Dynamic-import heavy libraries.
Destroy on unmount and verify with a heap snapshot.
Do not SSR the library's private DOM.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- Mount, update, and destroy imperative widgets explicitly.
- `markRaw` the instance. Do not proxy it.
- Vue must not patch the DOM the library owns.
- Client-only construction avoids SSR crashes and hydration fights.

Official references

- https://vuejs.org/guide/essentials/template-refs.html
- https://vuejs.org/guide/extras/reactivity-in-depth.html

title: Plugins and dynamic components
description: app.use, global registration, and how to load optional UI without a grab bag of globals.

blocks.title: A plugin installs into one app instance
blocks.content:
A Vue plugin is an object or function with `install(app, options)`. `app.use` runs it and dedupes that plugin object on that app. Inside `install` you may `app.provide`, `app.component`, `app.directive`, and `app.config.globalProperties`. Prefer provide/inject over `globalProperties`. Properties bolted onto the instance proxy show up as `this.$thing` in the Options API and are awkward in `<script setup>`, easy to overwrite, and invisible in a function's dependencies.

A plugin that fetches data at install time slows every test and every SSR request. Provide a factory or a client. Let the caller decide when to fetch.
keyPoints: `app.use` is per app. Tests and SSR requests that create a new app must install again.
Provide services. Do not hang them off `globalProperties` in new code.
Global components are for a small design system, not for feature pages.
Plugins should be idempotent for a given app instance.

blocks.title: Dynamic components need a closed registry
blocks.content:
`<component :is="view">` renders a component object or a registered name. A feature flag can choose between two components you imported. A CMS should not send a component name that maps onto the entire app. Build a registry: `{ hero: HeroBlock, faq: FaqBlock }`. Unknown keys render a fallback.

If the set is large, the values in the registry can be async components so the page does not download every block. The key of the registry is still data. The value is code you shipped.
keyPoints: Look up components in a local map.
Unknown keys get a fallback, not a crash in production if content is user-authored.
A missing registration is a dev error for your own code.
Do not pass a user string to a function that imports arbitrary paths.

blocks.title: Provide a client from a plugin
blocks.explanation: The app installs the plugin with a concrete client. Components call `useApi()` and tests provide a fake. Nothing is added to `globalProperties`, so `<script setup>` stays explicit.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: When is a plugin the wrong place for a feature?
blocks.answer:
When the feature has a route, a store, and screens. Those belong in a feature module that the router lazy-loads. A plugin is for cross-cutting infrastructure: an API client, an i18n instance, a small set of global directives. Putting the billing screens in `app.use(billing)` usually global-registers components and hides the dependency from the route graph.

I would also keep plugins free of order-sensitive side effects. If plugin B must run after plugin A, that coupling should be obvious in `main.ts`, not buried in import order.
blocks.explanation: Plugins install capabilities. Features are loaded by routes.

blocks.title: The plugin that ran once for two apps
blocks.question: A test creates two `createApp` roots. The API plugin uses a module-level `let installed = false` and returns early the second time. The second app's `useApi()` throws. Why?
blocks.answer: `app.use` dedupes per app, but the hand-rolled flag dedupes per JavaScript realm. The second app never received `provide`. Remove the flag and let `app.use` handle dedupe, or key the flag by the app instance. Tests and SSR both create more than one app.
blocks.explanation:
Install state belongs to the app instance. Module state is shared by every app in the page or test process.

[Further reading](https://vuejs.org/guide/reusability/plugins.html)
hints: What does a module-level boolean live as long as?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: A CMS returns block types for a landing page. Marketing can add new block names without a deploy. How do you render that safely?
blocks.answer:
You cannot render a block whose code has not shipped. The registry contains the types this deploy knows. Unknown names render a documented fallback and log the type so marketing sees they need a release. The CMS does not supply Vue code or a URL to import.

Optional blocks can be async components inside the registry so the landing route stays small. The allowlist is still compiled into the app.
blocks.explanation: Data selects from code you shipped. It does not become code.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Registering every view globally in `main.ts` so templates can use tags without imports.
blocks.whyItHappens: It copies the Vue 2 global component habit and defeats lazy routes because the views are imported up front.
blocks.correctApproach: Import components in the SFCs that use them. Globally register only true primitives, if anything.

blocks.title: Production guidance
blocks.content: Install infrastructure with plugins. Load features with routes. Select UI from a closed map.
keyPoints: Prefer `app.provide` to `globalProperties`.
Do not use a process-wide installed flag.
Keep global registration tiny.
Map content types to local components.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- `install(app)` runs per app instance.
- Provide services instead of adding `$globals`.
- Dynamic `:is` should read a local registry.
- Unknown CMS blocks need a fallback, not a remote import.

Official references

- https://vuejs.org/guide/reusability/plugins.html

title: Options API migration
description: How to move a living Vue codebase toward script setup without a freeze.

blocks.title: Both APIs are supported. Mixins are the expensive part.
blocks.content:
Vue 3 still runs the Options API. A component can use `data`, `computed`, `methods`, and `props` while its children use `<script setup>`. That is the migration path: new code uses script setup, and old code moves when you are already changing it. A repository-wide rewrite creates conflicts and regressions without a user-facing gain.

Mixins are the part that does not map cleanly. They share `data` keys implicitly, collide on method names, and are hard to type. Replace a mixin with a composable that returns explicit refs. Do that when you touch the feature, and delete the mixin once the last caller is gone. Leaving both the mixin and the composable updating the same field doubles the bugs.
keyPoints: Do not block feature work on a total conversion.
One component at a time, with its tests.
Replace mixins with composables that return values. Do not hide a mixin inside `setup`.
`this.$refs` and `this.$on` habits need a redesign, not a line-by-line port. Vue 3 removed the instance event bus.

blocks.title: Watch the behavior changes, not only the syntax
blocks.content:
Vue 3 `v-if` has higher priority than `v-for` on the same element. Filters in templates are gone, replaced by methods or computed. `Vue.set` is unnecessary for reactive objects. `$listeners` was merged into `$attrs`. A functional component written as an object is not the same as a function component in Vue 3.

The event bus (`new Vue()` as a bus, or `$on`) is gone. A tiny bus becomes an external library only if you truly need it. Most buses should become props, emits, or a store. Keeping an event bus "temporarily" for five years is how implicit coupling survives the migration.
keyPoints: Retest lists that used `v-for` and `v-if` together.
Replace filters and the event bus on purpose.
Reactive objects observe new keys. Do not keep `Vue.set` as cargo cult.
Measure bundle size after removing the compatibility build if you had been running Vue 2 compat.

blocks.title: Replace a mixin with a composable
blocks.explanation: Callers see `dirty` and `commit` in the return value. There is no implicit `this.dirty` from a mixin that another mixin might also define. The component decides how to bind `current` in the template.

blocks.title: Interview question
blocks.question: How would you plan a Vue 2 or Options API migration while the team still ships weekly?
blocks.answer:
I would inventory mixins, event buses, and `v-for`/`v-if` pairs, because those are behavior changes rather than syntax. I would upgrade to Vue 3 with the compatibility build only if we need it, with a dated removal. New components use `<script setup>`. Each touched Options component either stays or moves entirely in that PR, with its tests. I would not convert a stable component for style.

I would track remaining mixins and the compat build as visible debt, and I would ban new mixins in review.
blocks.explanation: The plan is risk-ordered. Syntax conversion is the cheap part. Implicit coupling is the expensive part.

blocks.title: The mixin and the composable both write the title
blocks.question: During migration a component still mixes in `pageTitle` and also calls `useTitle()`. Both set `document.title`. Users see the mixin title, then the composable title, depending on hook order. What should the PR do?
blocks.answer: One owner. Remove the mixin from this component in the same PR that adds `useTitle()`, and check the other mixin consumers before deleting the mixin file. Leaving both is not an incremental step. It is two writers.
blocks.explanation:
Incremental migration means one component fully moved, not two mechanisms stacked.

[Further reading](https://vuejs.org/guide/reusability/composables.html)
hints: Can both run in one component without a defined order?

blocks.title: Senior scenario
blocks.question: A five-year-old Vue 2 app uses a global event bus for "cart updated" and dozens of pages listen. Product wants Vue 3 this quarter. What do you replace the bus with first?
blocks.answer:
Introduce a small cart store and write to it from the same places that used to emit. Replace listeners with `storeToRefs` or a computed as you touch each page. Keep a temporary adapter that emits into the store so unmigrated listeners still work, and count those listeners in CI until the list is empty.

I would not search-and-replace `$on` with a third-party bus and call the migration done. The coupling stays invisible. I would also fix `v-if`/`v-for` templates while those pages are open.
blocks.explanation: The bus is a hidden store. Give it a name and delete the adapter on a schedule.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.mistake: Rewriting every component to `<script setup>` in one branch before the Vue 3 upgrade is even stable in CI.
blocks.whyItHappens: The diff looks like progress. It cannot be reviewed, and behavior changes hide inside the formatting.
blocks.correctApproach: Upgrade the runtime, get tests green, then move components when you change them. Review behavior diffs separately from formatting.

blocks.title: Production guidance
blocks.content: Migrate coupling first and syntax second.
keyPoints: Keep Options API components that are stable.
Replace mixins with composables one caller at a time.
Retest directive priority, filters, and `$attrs`.
Delete the event bus and the compat build on a schedule.

blocks.title: Quick revision and official references
blocks.content:
Quick revision

- Vue 3 runs Options API and `<script setup>` together.
- Mixins and event buses are the real migration cost.
- Do not leave a mixin and a composable writing the same state.
- `v-if` beats `v-for` on one element in Vue 3.

Official references

- https://vuejs.org/guide/introduction.html
- https://vuejs.org/guide/reusability/composables.html
- https://vuejs.org/guide/essentials/list.html
